claim: Clear Signing stewardship moved from Ledger to the Ethereum Foundation's Trillion Dollar Security Initiative on 2026-05-12 (registry now under github.com/ethereum, mirrorable; home clearsigning.org). The launch bundle is four parts: updated ERC-7730, an EF-hosted off-chain registry, ERC-8176 attestations on EAS, and Rust/TypeScript SDKs. Working group named: Ledger, Trezor, MetaMask, WalletConnect, Sourcify, Fireblocks, Cyfrin, Zama, Keycard, ZKnox, Argot. Registry inclusion explicitly does NOT mean a descriptor is safe or approved; wallets choose which attesters to trust. No primary source gives descriptor/wallet adoption counts (secondary press says '40+ protocols').
relevance: pq1's ERC7730_DESCRIPTORS_ROOT is built by dbgen from this registry. The registry's own position is 'inclusion != safe', so dbgen admission must require ERC-8176 attestations from a pinned attester set, not registry presence. The EF move also means the upstream URL/governance pq1 pins has changed since the curation was last re-bound.

claim: ERC-8176 (Draft, created 2026-02-26) attests only a descriptorHash = keccak256 of the fully resolved, RFC 8785-canonicalised descriptor, via a permissionless EAS schema (`bytes32 descriptorHash`, no resolver, anyone can attest); on-chain or off-chain EIP-712 attestations; EOA attesters verified by ECDSA recovery, contract attesters via ERC-1271. The spec states 'Wallets are responsible for maintaining the set of attesters they trust' and 'Signature verification does not validate semantic correctness'; malicious attesters, key compromise and semantic descriptor errors are explicit non-protections. The 2026-09-23 registry sync call records that 'Attestations are brittle: any small descriptor change (label, new deployment, removed deployment) invalidates the hash', 'Human auditing does not scale. Most review will go through AI plus deterministic checks', and 'The registry disclaimer does not cover auditors'.
relevance: Matches CLAUDE.md's model (dbgen verifies externally mandated EAS/secp256k1 attestations to admit catalogue inputs; the firmware never holds the key). Risk to pq1: attestation churn means the pinned clear set C will drift stale quickly; and an attestation proves review of bytes, not intent, so the catalogue admission gate still needs pq1's own render-faithfulness tests per descriptor.

claim: ERC-7730 spec security considerations: 'ERC-7730 creates a risk surface where malicious actors could abuse formatting to make unsafe transactions appear benign'; registry curation is out of scope and 'any external registry or wallet ecosystem MUST assume it will be targeted'; descriptors for upgradeable proxies 'SHOULD be bound to the proxy address' and developers 'SHOULD update the ERC-7730 file' on upgrade (so a stale descriptor can silently describe old behaviour); interpolatedIntent: 'Very long formatted values could push critical information off-screen', interpolation MUST fail if a path lacks a field format, and 'Hardware wallets ... MAY choose not to implement interpolatedIntent support'; recursive `calldata` formatters 'are expected to work with restrictions at first'. The 2026-09 sync call adds Trezor's verdict on proxies: 'very difficult for hardware as written' and Trezor 'does not sign for that proxy' when implementations differ in intent; Nicolas Bacca warned 'a two-tier display (software wallet shows more than the device) is dangerous'.
relevance: Directly informs pq1's descriptor admission: (a) bind descriptors to proxy address AND pin the implementation codehash/era in the catalogue so an upgrade invalidates the descriptor instead of mis-rendering; (b) never implement interpolatedIntent on the 16x4/pixel UI (off-screen truncation is a WYSIWYS failure); (c) pq1's 'companion never shows more than the device' rule is validated by the Ledger CTO's own warning.

claim: Trezor shipped ERC-7730 clear signing in Universal firmware 2.12.2 (2026-07-22, 'Improved clear signing support' #6733; issue closed 2026-09-29 'Done (no QA)') for Model T/Safe 3/5/7. Design, from the firmware source: descriptors are host-supplied signed blobs (same `trzd` Merkle-tree + CoSi-signed-root envelope as token definitions, 'must be cryptographically signed by Trezor company'); built-ins are only ERC-20 approve/transfer and WETH deposit/withdraw; nested `calldata` depth is capped at 1; `@.from` and `@.value` are rejected when nested because 'the device cannot tell' whether the wrapper CALLs or DELEGATECALLs the callee; multicall `bytes[]` arrays are unsupported; the response to a definition request is pinned to (selector, chain, callee) so a validly-signed blob for another function cannot be substituted; zero-field tuples are rejected to stop an attacker-controlled length word driving an unbounded parse loop; _MAX_ABI_NESTING/_MAX_NESTED_ARRAYS bound aliasing blow-up (3 array levels ~250k values within 6144 B).
relevance: Three concrete checks for pq1's host-moved ERC-7730 renderer (pqsigner-erc7730): (1) offset-aliasing in nested dynamic arrays multiplies decoded output N×M — verify pq1's walker bounds total decoded values, not just calldata length; (2) `@.from`/`@.value` inside nested calldata are semantically unknowable without knowing CALL vs DELEGATECALL — pq1 should refuse (it already does for Safe op=1 outside MultiSendCallOnly; extend to generic nested calldata); (3) binding the descriptor response to the exact (chain, callee, selector) request is the same anti-substitution property pq1 gets from Merkle-root pinning — keep it a hard refusal.

claim: Trezor's fallback on any clear-signing failure is blind signing, not refusal: 'All parsing errors derive from ClearSigningFailed. sign_tx catches it and falls back to blind signing - the transaction can still be signed'; calldata larger than _MAX_DATA_STORED = 6144 bytes 'is never clear-signed' because streaming more data 'would not be able to fall back to blind signing anymore'; the user guide says unregistered contracts show 'the hash or Data Present ... accompanied by the usual warning'. Ledger's wallet docs likewise: 'If no descriptor exists for the target contract, the signer falls back to blind signing' (also for signTypedData), and Ledger's app security requirements say 'If blind signing is implemented, it must be disabled by default' and the device 'should be rejected ... unless the user has acknowledged that they will be blind signing'. Neither vendor hard-refuses a registry-known shape that fails to decode.
relevance: This is the exact design seam where pq1 already surpasses both vendors: 'a tuple in the accepted clear set C either clear-signs or fatal-refuses'. Keep it, and document it as a differentiator with these citations. The 6144-B Trezor cap vs pq1's 4096-B data_len also suggests pq1 should state its own 'never clear-sign above N bytes' bound explicitly rather than let a page-budget overflow be the only refusal path.

claim: Trezor firmware 2.12.4 (2026-08-19) added 'experimental support for EIP-7702 authorization/revocation' that refuses rather than blind-signs: chain_id 0 raises 'EIP-7702: cross-chain delegation'; non-empty calldata, non-zero value and unknown network are DataErrors; the authorization nonce is forced to tx.nonce + 1 (self-sponsored only); and a delegate not in the compiled-in allowlist (`lookup_eip7702_address`, currently Simple7702Account deployments) raises 'Unknown EIP-7702 delegate address'. This matches Ambire's Jan-29-2025 report that 'both teams [Trezor and Ledger] told us that they'd only implement such a feature if they had an allow-list of audited designator contracts'. Ledger app-ethereum 1.22.3 (Aug 2026) fixed 'EIP-7702 authorizations without a chain ID were accepted for all chains' and 'EIP-7702 authorization review could be tricked into signing with a different key than displayed'.
relevance: pq1 keys are never EOAs (4337 smart account), so a 7702 authorization over a pq1 key is meaningless and there is no CMD for it — document that this is a structural refusal, and add a negative test that any attempt to route a 7702 tuple (magic 0x05) through SIGN_OFFCHAIN RAW32 is impossible because the firmware keccak-nests before signing. Ledger's two 7702 bugs (chain-id-0 wildcard, displayed-key != signing-key) are exactly the class pq1's render-faithfulness tests should pin for chain_id and account_index on every dialog.

claim: Ledger Security Bulletin 024 (published 2026-08-27, classified High on 2026-04-23): the Ethereum app's Generic Transaction Parser 'stored an attacker-controlled 16-bit array element count in an 8-bit countdown field', so 257 elements wrapped to 1 and 'the device reviewed only the final element while its signature still authorised the complete transaction'. Affected 1.19.0–1.22.2, fixed in 1.22.3 (2026-08-25); requires a compromised host and a descriptor iterating an attacker-controlled array >255 elements; blind signing was NOT required; 'the primary threat is a compromised multisig frontend'. Validated on a private fork: a 257-operation batch signed after one operation was displayed. Note 1.22.2 was tagged 2026-08-13 without the fix.
relevance: Highest-value external lesson for pq1's multiSend/batch/ERC-7730 array paths: the signed bytes covered more than the displayed records. pq1's defences (≤6 records, exact framing, page-budget overflow = refusal) are the right shape; add a Kani/proptest that for every array formatter the rendered element count equals the decoded element count and that any narrowing cast is bounds-checked, and make 'displayed elements == signed elements' an explicit paired-constant invariant.

claim: Ledger Ethereum app 1.22.2 (patched 2026-08-12, no advisory; publicly disclosed by TestMachine 2026-08-21/23) fixed an APDU race condition in clear-signing flows that 'could have allowed a second, malicious APDU command to slip in and replace the original transaction data' between review and signature, so a user approving a small transfer could sign an unlimited approval; Ledger says Donjon found it with AI-assisted tools. Separately LSB-025 (same day): the swap flow checked address and quantity 'but not the nature of the operation being requested', so an ERC-20 approve 'was signed without being displayed' in place of a payment (1.20.0–1.22.2, fixed 1.22.3). 1.22.0 release notes list 'Blind-signing bypass for single-byte calldata 0x00 transactions' and 'Blind-signing bypass with EIP-712 filtering activation'; 1.22.3 adds 'EIP-712 messages with recursive structures could crash the device' and 'Legacy transactions vulnerable to cross-chain replay are now rejected'.
relevance: Three pq1 checks: (1) TOCTOU between display and sign — pq1 copies NS buffers to S-stack before parse, but confirm the signed digest is computed from the SAME S-world copy that was rendered and that no further NSC/USB call can mutate state between confirm() and c10_sign_verified (the 120 s idle timer and the gateway dispatcher must be mutually exclusive during a dialog); (2) selector-binding: every ladder rung must dispatch on the 4-byte selector, never on 'address+amount shape' (LSB-025 class); (3) a zero-length/`0x00` calldata must not be classified as 'plain value transfer' — add that negative case to the value-transfer page tests.

claim: Ledger Transaction Check (available 'today on Ledger Stax and Ledger Flex devices for Ethereum transactions in Ledger Live') sends the transaction to off-device simulation providers (Blockaid's Transaction Security Engine; a May 2025 report also names Cyvers) and 'a cryptographically signed summary of the result is delivered directly to the Ledger device, where the user sees a clear warning or a green light, with a link to the full security report'. Blockaid's page does not say who signs the summary, does not say whether flagged transactions are blocked, and gives no privacy statement. MetaMask's Blockaid alerts likewise 'do not block' — the user can still confirm.
relevance: Simulation verdicts are an off-device oracle that the device can only verify as 'signed by provider X', not as true. If pq1 ever adds a risk-verdict input it should be refuse-only (a signed 'critical' verdict can block; a 'green' verdict can never unlock a blind path) and must not leak the UserOp to a third party before the user has seen it on the trusted display.

claim: Transaction-simulation phishing is a measured attack class: the arXiv paper 'Blockchain Transaction Simulation Phishing' (2607.28747, July 2026) identifies >4,000 phishing contracts deployed Aug 2024–Jun 2025 across Ethereum/BSC/Avalanche/Polygon, ~$3.48M losses (upper bound), 91.5% on Ethereum, with one cluster of 268 contracts taking ~83% of losses; the mechanism is a TOCTOU race where the attacker changes contract state (e.g. blacklists the victim) between the wallet's simulation and execution. Scam Sniffer documented a Jan-2025 case where the victim signed 30 s after the state change and lost 143.35 ETH. Proposed mitigations are all re-simulation triggers (state change, gas limit, gas price, block number/timestamp), i.e. the defence remains probabilistic.
relevance: Evidence for pq1's design choice of on-device semantic decoding over simulation: a simulated 'you receive 0.1 ETH' is not a property of the signed bytes. pq1 should state in the threat model that it renders *intent* (what the calldata asks for), never *outcome*, and must not present any simulation-derived balance delta on the trusted display.

claim: Scam Sniffer's 2025 wallet-drainer report: $83.85M lost across 106,106 victims (down 83% / 68% vs 2024's $494M), EVM phishing-site drainers only (lower bound). Of the 11 cases over $1M ($22.98M total): Permit/Permit2 3 cases $8.72M, approve/increaseApproval 3 cases $5.62M, transfer 2 cases $4.87M, EIP-7702 batch 2 cases $2.54M, setApprovalForAll 1 case $1.23M. Largest single theft: $6.5M via a Permit signature (September). 'EIP-7702 malicious signatures emerged after the Pectra upgrade, with 2 large cases in August.'
relevance: Off-chain EIP-712 permits remain the dominant single-signature drain vector. pq1's CMD_SIGN_OFFCHAIN EIP712_TYPED path should carry native decoders for EIP-2612 `Permit` and Uniswap Permit2 `PermitSingle`/`PermitBatch`/`PermitTransferFrom` (spender, token, amount with 'UNLIMITED' banner, deadline/expiration as date) and refuse unknown typed-data domains outright; RAW32 must never be the companion's path for a permit (CLAUDE.md already forbids downgrade — add a test that a Permit2 domain submitted as RAW32 is refused when the hash matches a known-domain preimage shape).

claim: EIP-7702 delegation phishing is measured at scale: arXiv 2512.12174 (Dec 2025) analyses >150k authorization/execution events over 26k addresses and 'hundreds of delegator contracts', finding authorizations 'dominated by a small number of contract families linked to criminal activity' with three trigger pathways (user-driven, attacker-driven, protocol-triggered). Secondary reporting of a USENIX Security '26 study: 2,322,548 of 3,664,166 authorization transactions across seven chains through 2025-07-15 (63%) were attacker-linked, 924 malicious contracts confirmed, ~$2.36M confirmed losses, and attackers 'rebinding accounts to benign code after an attack'. Relay and TokenPocket note most wallet UIs cannot show what a delegation means and revocation tooling misses account-level delegations.
relevance: pq1 is immune to 7702 on its own keys (no EOA), which is a sellable property the EOA-based hardware wallets cannot claim. The residual is upstream: a hostile companion could feed pq1 a UserOp whose *inner call* targets a 7702-delegated counterparty; nothing to decode there, but the docs should state the boundary honestly.

claim: Bybit (2025-02-21, >$1.4B, 401,347 ETH): NCC Group's analysis shows injected Safe{Wallet} JavaScript that activated only when the signer was a Bybit address and operation was 0, swapped `to`, `data`, `operation` (to 1 = DELEGATECALL), `value` and `safeTxGas`, obtained the tampered signature, then restored the original data before proposal. The delegatecall target 0x9622...7242 exposed a fake ERC-20 `transfer` that wrote the attacker address into storage slot 0 (the proxy implementation). Hardware wallets received the tampered EIP-712 message but 'the underlying data is not human-readable'. Safe Gateway afterwards added a check that 'the signature matches the proposed transaction'; NCC notes 'JavaScript pinning would have prevented the attack'. Bybit's CEO said the device showed 'a lot of code'.
relevance: pq1's SafeTx path (operation=1 accepted only against three pinned MultiSendCallOnly deployments, otherwise refusal) is exactly the control that would have stopped Bybit; note the attacker's payload *looked like* `transfer(address,uint256)` — a naive ERC-20 decoder that ignores `operation` would have rendered a benign transfer. Keep `operation` as a first-class, always-displayed field and add a regression test using the Bybit calldata as a must-refuse vector.

claim: Radiant Capital (Oct 2024, ~$50M): per the post-mortem as relayed by Hacken and crypto.news, malware on at least three developers' machines manipulated the Safe{Wallet} front-end 'displaying legitimate transaction data to the developers while executing malicious transactions in the background'; because Ledger devices 'do not parse Gnosis Safe transactions' the signers blind-signed a `transferOwnership()`; attackers exploited routine Safe transaction resubmissions (gas/congestion errors) to 'collect multiple compromised signatures unnoticed'; Tenderly simulations and manual review detected nothing; the recommendations include an independent verification device and avoiding blind signing for critical transactions.
relevance: Two pq1 levers beyond decoding: (1) the 'retry after failure' social pattern — pq1 should display Safe nonce prominently and could count/flag repeated sign requests for the same (Safe, nonce) within a session; (2) the trusted-display device IS the independent verification device only if it decodes — Safe owner changes already render on pq1, so make `transferOwnership`/`swapOwner`/`addOwnerWithThreshold` a loud red-banner class rather than an ordinary management page.

claim: The current industry SOP for Safe signing on hardware wallets is manual hash comparison, not decoding: SEAL's framework says 'Message Hash on tools must match hardware wallet display', 'Domain Hash ensures correct Safe', 'verify the entire hash displayed on your hardware wallet, not just the first and last few characters', and DELEGATECALL 'Should only appear when the target is a known, audited module'; Safe's own guide has users compare `safeTxHash` from the Safe backend and Etherscan `getTransactionHash` against the device, with a Ledger-specific hex/`0x`-stripping conversion step; tools are pcaversaccio's safe-tx-hashes-util (Cyfrin fork `safe_hashes`) and OpenZeppelin's web wrapper, which itself states it 'has not been subject to any security assessment'.
relevance: pq1 already decodes SafeTx on-device, which obsoletes this SOP; but Safe-savvy users will still want to cross-check with safe_hashes. Rendering domainSeparator, hashStruct(SafeTx) and safeTxHash on a final trailer page (cheap, already computed in S-world) gives those users a zero-cost second channel and matches ERC-8213.

claim: ERC-8213 'Wallet Signature and Calldata Digest Display' (Patrick Collins/Cyfrin; thread opened 2025-05-21, ERC number assigned 2026-03-31) defines calldataDigest = keccak256(len(calldata) as 32-byte BE || calldata) and the EIP-712 digest ('\x19\x01' || domainSeparator || hashStruct), deliberately omitting chainId/deadline; wallets 'should always offer to show' them. The author concedes 'this ERC does not solve blind signing' and targets technically capable users; MicahZoltu's critique: 'just showing the user a digest or hash of any kind is not going to help much'. Keycard Shell is cited as the first wallet implementing it; Cyfrin calls it 'a weaker but always-applicable guarantee' and 'isn't a replacement for descriptor coverage'.
relevance: pq1's `erc8213.rs` fingerprint pages are aligned with the standard's own framing: a verifiability fallback, never a semantic claim. Keep it loud ('! BLIND') and ensure the length-prefix encoding matches the reference (32-byte BE length) so external tools agree byte-for-byte.

claim: The ERC-7730 ecosystem is adding (a) ERC-8283, a draft on-chain registry contract with 'No gatekeeping, no maintainer' where anyone can write and trust derives solely from ERC-8176 attestations, looked up by a computed contextId; (b) a compact binary wire format: the sync call records 'Adapt the CBOR draft using Trezor's protobuf definitions. The universal signer will be the first client'; (c) per-function descriptor files; (d) a Sourcify 'canary' second attestation and a CI pipeline of deterministic checks plus 'a basic AI review'; (e) Ledger's open-sourced Linter/Tester/Analyzer (LLM-powered audit)/Generator (LLM-powered generation from source code). ERC-7730 v2 adds cross-chain support and collapses 'dozens of separate ERC7730 definitions' for ERC-4626 vaults; Ledger's tools and registry 'currently target ERC-7730 v1, while v2 is in draft'.
relevance: Two actions: dbgen should be able to source descriptors from the on-chain registry + attestation set so catalogue admission is reproducible from chain state, not a GitHub snapshot; and pq1's descriptor TLV should track the emerging CBOR/protobuf device wire format so pq1 can consume the same signed blobs Trezor does. Treat LLM-generated descriptors as untrusted input — admission must require a human/attested review, not generator provenance.

claim: ERC-4337 UserOperation signing has no clear-signing standard: the Ethereum Magicians `eth_signUserOperation` thread (Oct 2023) states the reference implementation uses personalSign over the userOpHash, 'Wallets do not show warnings on personalSign, even when signing 32 bytes which could be a transaction hash', 'Using personalSign makes it near impossible for wallets to tell users what they are signing', and thirdweb's engineer: 'there is no way we could recommend using 4337 with an existing wallet like MM or CB wallet because of this ... The only reasonable solution was to hide this uglyness away with an embedded/local wallet'. Dapp-supplied paymaster data and gas values have no path into a wallet signing request. No Ledger/Trezor UserOp decoding was found in any vendor source.
relevance: pq1 is, per these sources, ahead of every shipping hardware wallet on 4337: the firmware takes the full UserOp field set, recomputes userOpHash in S-world, and decodes the inner call. Gap to close honestly: pq1 receives only `paymaster_and_data_hash` and gas limits — the device cannot show WHO sponsors or what the paymaster calldata authorises (e.g. an ERC-20 fee-token paymaster that pulls tokens). Either render the paymaster address + a decoded fee-token amount, or state that paymaster semantics are out of the clear-sign guarantee.

claim: GridPlus Lattice1 decodes calldata on-device 'automatically for all contracts ... starting in Lattice firmware v0.15.0', but the ABI source is the requester fetching verified source from Etherscan, with 4byte as fallback (4byte 'does not include parameter names'); nested ABI decoding goes 'two layers' with generic labels '[#1], [#1-1]' because the device 'cannot request nested parameter names from Etherscan, which requires an address'; when neither source has it the device does not decode and users should be 'extra skeptical'. Keystone's Smart-Contract-Metadata-Registry is a community JSON-per-address ABI set (proxies filed under the implementation ABI, 'please fill the abi of your origin contract') with no stated signing/verification; Keystone's firmware README only claims 'safeguards against blind signing'.
relevance: Both vendors render names from unauthenticated or lightly-curated ABI sources (Etherscan/4byte collisions, community JSON), so their 'decoded' view is not WYSIWYS-grade. pq1's Merkle-root-pinned descriptors are stronger provenance; the one idea worth borrowing is Lattice's type-only nested decoding — for a registry-unknown inner call pq1 could show typed, labelled-by-position arguments (address/uint) as a loud non-semantic fallback instead of a raw hex blob, without claiming intent.

claim: Trezor's token/network definition supply chain: external definitions are protobuf blobs in a `trzd` envelope (magic, format version, type, data version, payload) carrying a Merkle proof to a root signed with CoSi; the Merkle tree uses SHA256(0x00||leaf) and SHA256(0x01||min||max); 'A given Trezor firmware will only accept signed definitions newer than a certain date, typically one month before firmware release'; a subset is baked into firmware (networks.json/tokens.json); data sources are CoinGecko, defillama, ethereum-lists. Format v2 reduced the required CoSi signatures from 2 to 1.
relevance: pq1's ERC20_DB_ROOT / ERC7730_DESCRIPTORS_ROOT are compiled-in, so freshness is bound to firmware updates (and invariant #10 makes updates something the user should not have to trust). Trezor's model shows the alternative: signed, time-floored external definitions. A middle path for pq1 is a vendor-signed (SPHINCS+C10 — invariant #5 permits one algorithm) descriptor-root update with a monotonic data-version floor pinned in flash, so the catalogue can refresh without a firmware image change; note Trezor's reduction to a single CoSi signer as a provenance weakening to avoid.

claim: 'Enforceable Human-Readable Transactions' (ethresear.ch, GCdePaula, 2025-02-26) proposes that the user signs 'the message, which includes both the incomprehensible input data and its alleged description', the front end strips the description before submission, and the contract 'reconstructs the description' deterministically and verifies the signature: 'If the description is incorrect, the signature verification will fail'. MicahZoltu linked EIP-719 (Trustless Signing UI Protocol: a DSL whose hash the signer checks against the target contract) and argued on-device translation 'is impractical for small devices' and that 4-byte selectors are 'incredibly lossy'; Phle-bas argued developer-assigned descriptions add attack surface.
relevance: A genuinely novel lever available to pq1 but not to Ledger/Trezor: pq1 controls BOTH the signer and the wallet contract. PQSmartWallet's `executeWithOffchainCount` could commit, in the signed sphincsDigest, to a hash of the exact ASCII intent pages the device rendered (or a canonical description derived on-chain from calldata), so a signature over an undisplayed intent cannot validate on-chain. This turns WYSIWYS from a device property into an on-chain-enforced one. Cost: calldata/gas and a canonical description grammar; worth a design spike.

claim: 'What I Sign Is Not What I See' (arXiv 2601.16751, Jan 2026, cs.HC/cs.CR): two formative studies found users 'misread critical parameters', 'underestimate high-risk signatures' and 'rely on superficial familiarity rather than understanding transaction intent'; a between-subjects study (N=128) of a 'Signature Semantic Decoder' that reconstructs intent with risk cues produced higher accuracy identifying risky signatures, higher clarity/confidence and lower cognitive workload than a baseline wallet UI. No effect sizes are given on the abstract page.
relevance: Empirical support for pq1's intent-banner-first page order and the 2026-09-24 scroll-to-end decision; it also argues that hash/digest pages (RAW32, ERC-8213) should carry an explicit risk cue rather than neutral hex, since 'familiarity' is what attackers exploit.

claim: Safe Research's Policy Engine (2025-10-21) is 'an onchain mandatory access control system for Safe transactions': a `SafePolicyGuard` installed via setGuard maps an access selector (e.g. 'DELEGATECALL to SafeMultiSendCallOnly.multiSend()') to policy contracts, with 'wildcard fallback selectors for any CALL or any DELEGATECALL', and 'If no policy approves, the transaction is denied'; audit/deployment status is not stated. Ackee's post-Bybit guidance: a ScopeGuard that reverts 'Delegate call not allowed to this address', 'Start using a guard that prevents delegate calls', 'There is always one Guard, and it can only block transactions'.
relevance: Defence in depth for pq1 users who cosign Safes: pq1's device-side refusal of op=1 outside pinned MultiSendCallOnly should be mirrored by recommending (in companion docs) a guard with the same allowlist, so a compromised cosigner set cannot do what pq1 refuses. For PQSmartWallet itself, confirm there is no delegatecall-equivalent execution path at all and state it as an invariant.

claim: Ledger's ERC-7730 v2 post (2026-05-15) frames the limit of trusted displays: 'even a secure screen cannot prevent blind signing' without structured metadata; Ledger devices clear-sign 'simple transfers of native currency or tokens' natively and everything else only with descriptors; Ledger says Ledger Wallet, Ledger Enterprise Multisig and Ledger Direct Access implement Clear Signing and that 'Both the wallet and the dApp must support ERC-7730 for the details to display'. Trezor's launch coverage lists 1inch, Aave, Lido, Tether, LiFi and Hyperliquid as initial descriptor publishers (secondary source).
relevance: Coverage, not display, is the binding constraint for both incumbents; pq1's ERC-7730 pack coverage (a stated selling point per memory) should be measured against the registry's priority dashboard and reported as a number in docs, with the refused-known set F enumerated.

claim: EIP-7896 (Francisco Giordano, created 2025-02-27, status Stagnant) proposed extending EIP-5792 `wallet_sendCalls` with an `interfaces` capability so a dapp can attach contract ABIs (abi-v1/abi-v2) for the wallet to decode calldata; its Security Considerations are 'Needs discussion'. Separately, Trezor's clear-signing design requires descriptors to be 'cryptographically signed by Trezor company' and resolved by the host at signing time because 'Storing all of them in firmware is not feasible'.
relevance: Dapp-supplied ABIs (EIP-7896) are untrusted by construction and the proposal stalled — pq1 should not accept companion-supplied descriptors/ABIs without a Merkle inclusion proof against the pinned root. Trezor's 'host resolves, device verifies signature + binding' model is the right delivery pattern if pq1 moves descriptors out of the image.

claim: Coldcard Mk4/Mk5/Q split the wallet secret across the STM32 MCU, an ATECC608B (SE1, holds the AES-256-CTR-encrypted seed) and a DS28C36B (SE2, holds Trick PINs and part of the decryption key); the AES key is an HMAC-SHA256 combination of three parts so 'both SE1 and SE2, plus the main micro need to be fully cracked to get the seed phrase out'. The genuine/caution LED is 'controlled by the secure element and enforced cryptographically' and 'any change to the flash memory of the MCU will also cause the red light to turn on'; the circuit is exposed on the top of the clear-case PCB so an implant or LED bypass is visible.
relevance: pq1 already has a two-SE XOR split (invariant #1) but no SE-gated, software-unforgeable boot-integrity indicator: the FSBL fingerprint is rendered by firmware on the LCD. An SE-driven LED (OPTIGA/SE050 GPIO or a hardware line that only toggles after the SE verifies a boot MAC over flash) is a cheap second channel that a malicious NS/S image cannot fake, and the clear-case/exposed-circuit choice is a shipped anti-implant visibility measure pq1 could adopt for the EVT enclosure.

claim: Coldcard 'anti-phishing words': after the PIN prefix, SE1 computes HMAC-SHA256 over the hashed prefix with a per-device secret and shows two BIP-39 words; a 2-second per-prefix rate limit means exhausting ~4M combinations takes ~93 days; it exists to detect 'a trojan-horse COLDCARD'. Foundation Passport Prime ships the same idea as 'Security Words' (off by default): two words after the first four PIN digits, derived from device identity and the Master Key, 'to ensure no one can tamper with or swap out your device during use'.
relevance: pq1's PIN entry happens in the S-world trusted UI but gives the user no proof that the device in hand is their device before they type the full PIN (a swapped/implanted unit can harvest the PIN). A prefix-keyed word pair computed inside OPTIGA/SE050 (e.g. CMAC over prefix with a per-device SE secret, rate-limited by the SE) adds an evil-maid/swap detector at near-zero cost and complements the boot fingerprint.

claim: Coldcard Trick PINs (stored in SE2): Brick Self ('will only display the word Bricked forever'), Countdown & Brick (covert, 5 min to 28 days), Silent Wipe, Wipe & Reboot, Look Blank, Just Reboot, Duress Wallet, Delta Mode (produces incorrect signatures for an attacker who knows the target wallet), Policy Unlock & Wipe. 'After 13 failed PIN attempts the COLDCARD will always brick itself, regardless of any other settings.' Coinkite warns an attacker who opens the case and watches the chip traffic 'could detect that this is a Trick PIN'.
relevance: pq1 has a duress PIN and a 10-wrong-PIN brick but not the covert countdown-to-brick, delta mode, or 'look blank' variants. Delta mode maps naturally to pq1: a duress account_index that signs valid-looking but wrong-key C10 signatures. The Coinkite caveat (bus traffic reveals trick vs real PIN) is a reminder that pq1's SCP03/Shielded tunnels must make the duress and real unlock paths traffic-indistinguishable.

claim: Coldcard SSSP (Single Signer Spending Policy) is a device-enforced policy: max magnitude per tx, velocity ('minimum number of blocks between spends', measured via nLockTime of the last signed PSBT), a 25-address whitelist with change auto-whitelisted, optional web 2FA (TOTP), and a lockdown where 'the COLDCARD cannot view or change the spending policy or any settings', seed words cannot be exported and firmware changes are disabled; 'violations found in a PSBT are not explained, just denied'. Threat model: 'you should assume the attacker already has your Main PIN'.
relevance: Clear-signing shows the user what they sign; it does not stop a coerced or careless user. An S-world policy engine over the unified-sign input (max value, allowlisted to_address/chain_id, min nonce/time gap, a separate Policy Unlock PIN whose compromise cannot export the seed) is orthogonal to pq1's ERC-7730 work and directly addresses the $5-wrench and compromised-companion cases. It needs only page-123-style durable state, no new per-signature flash beyond what invariant #9 allows if folded into the existing log.

claim: Coldcard 2021-2026 RNG failure (Block analysis): board headers set MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG to 0 and libngu guarded with '#ifndef', which 'verifies only that the macro exists. It does not reject a macro whose value is zero', so seeds came from a deterministic Yasmarang PRNG seeded from 'UID_low32 ^ SysTick->VAL' and XORed with a second public-constant stream ('XOR does not create entropy'). Mk4's secure-element reseed hashed 32 B from SE1 + 8 B from SE2 but 'only four digest bytes reach reseed()', bounding outputs at 2^32. The libngu health check only 'rejects adjacent repeated rng_get() outputs' and the wallet check only asserted >4 distinct bytes, so tests passed. Coinkite estimated ~40 bits (Mk3) and ~72 bits (Mk4/Mk5/Q); hotfixes 4.2.0 / 5.6.0 / 1.5.0Q shipped July 31 2026 and 'does not fix an already created seed phrase'.
relevance: The largest hardware-wallet loss of 2026 was a build-configuration bug, not a physical attack. pq1 bans software PRNGs but has no gate proving the TRNG path is actually linked and used at seed-wizard time. Concrete gates: (a) a link-time/CI assertion that the seed path calls hw::rng and no fallback symbol exists; (b) NIST SP 800-90B continuous health tests (repetition count + adaptive proportion) on the TRNG; (c) a host-side differential test that two wizard runs with identical UID/SysTick diverge; (d) full-digest reseeding of any DRBG; (e) require user-supplied entropy (dice/key presses) mixed in, as Coldcard does.

claim: Ledger Donjon (FDTC 2023, Abdellatif & Hériveaux) extracted locked user pages from the DeepCover DS28C36 (Coldcard Mk4's SE2) with double laser fault injection, after a Welch t-test over 100K locked vs 100K unlocked power traces located the two moments where the page-protection bit is handled: 'Single laser pulse is not efficient', 'Multiple faults seem to be required'. The attack 'is applicable on all the user pages (Coldcard Mk4)' but not on permanent-protected P256 private-key pages. Conclusions: 'Using double verification against Fault Injection attacks is not efficient enough if it is used alone', manufacturers 'must at minimum combine it with hardware and/or software jitter', and 'we recommend splitting secrets into shares between different circuits'.
relevance: Directly validates pq1's XOR split across two vendors' SEs (invariant #1), and warns that pq1's CfiCounter double-compute/compare gates are insufficient alone against a t-test-guided double fault: add random timing jitter (TRNG-driven dummy cycles) around every FI-critical compare, PIN-counter precharge, and SE response parse. Also a method pq1's own bench (Scaffold + Rigol, lascar/scared skills) can replicate on OPTIGA/SE050 traffic to find its own protection-bit windows.

claim: Ledger Donjon recovered the ESP32-V3 flash-encryption AES-256 key of a Blockstream Jade by CPA on the power trace of boot-time flash decryption: after localizing decryption via SNR on flash traffic, ~500K traces collected in 2 hours on a real Jade (ESP32 removed) recovered all key bytes but Key[0] (brute-forced). Decrypted firmware can be replaced with code that 'performs transactions to substituted addresses' (evil maid). Reported Oct 2021, Espressif advisory May 2022, Black Hat USA 2022.
relevance: pq1 relies on STM32U5 SAES with DHUK/BHK to wrap SE050's BHK (page 126) and derive the OPTIGA PBS. ST markets SAES as DPA-resistant, but pq1 has not measured it. A TVLA/CPA campaign on the first-boot SAES-CMAC(DHUK) and page-126 unwrap (boot-time, attacker-triggerable by power-cycling, exactly Jade's setting) is the single highest-value SCA experiment; a leak there turns a stolen device into a decryptable one.

claim: Blockstream Jade's 'Virtual Secure Element' / blind oracle: three secrets are needed to decrypt the recovery phrase (user PIN, a device unit key for which 'No firmware path exports that device key', and an oracle share). Jade sends a nested-HMAC derivative of the PIN mixed with the unit key so the oracle 'never receives the PIN'; the server stores only a SHA-256 of the PIN-derived secret, an encrypted key share and an attempt counter; 'The attempt counter lives on the server', and 'On the third wrong PIN, both destroy their copies'. The oracle is open source and self-hostable (Docker, Tor); fallback is SeedQR entry. Blockstream concedes the ESP32 'isn't hardened silicon'.
relevance: Coldcard's own statement is that cracking all three chips yields the seed. A remote blind share is the only shipped design where full physical compromise of every chip on the board is still insufficient without a network interaction that enforces an attempt counter the attacker cannot reset. For pq1 this could be an optional fourth XOR share held by a self-hosted oracle (companion relays blinded, PQ-KEM-wrapped messages), gating reconstruction of entropy in S-SRAM; it would also neutralise the E120/page-124 reconciliation-gap residual.

claim: Anti-exfil / anti-klepto: Jade (since firmware 0.1.24, 2021-04-14) makes the device 'use its signature nonce while cryptographically committing to some random data' supplied by the host, so a compromised wallet cannot 'leak parts of the user's master private key into individual nonces'; BitBox02 ships the same 'anti-klepto' protocol against the nonce covert channel.
relevance: SPHINCS+ has an analogous subliminal channel: the randomizer R = PRF(sk_prf, OptRand, M) lets malicious firmware pick OptRand to encode key bits across signatures, and C10's target-sum grinding adds a second degree of freedom. pq1 should either (a) derive OptRand deterministically from a host-supplied commitment (companion sends c, device uses OptRand = H(c || M) and returns a proof the host can check against R), or (b) document the residual explicitly. This is a firmware-supply-chain (malicious update / implant) defence that no PQ wallet ships yet.

claim: BitBox02 / BitBox02 Nova (datasheet): 'Encrypted seed stored on the MCU, protected by both the secure chip and user-chosen device password'; 'Monotonic counter in secure chip to avoid brute force attacks by limiting attempts'; 'Password stretching in secure chip'; 'Bootloader accepts only firmware signed by BitBox', 'Bootloader can display the hash of the firmware before running it for binary transparency', 'Bootloader prevents firmware downgrades', 'Device attestation to detect counterfeits'. Nova's secure chip is 'OPTIGA Trust M V3' (EAL6+, no NDA) with the attempt limit enforced by a hardware counter rather than the original BitBox02's firmware counter; BLE runs on a separate DA14531 chip.
relevance: Nova is a shipping precedent for pq1's exact OPTIGA Trust M V3 counter-gated PIN design, useful as an existence proof that the E120-style approach reaches production. The 'bootloader shows the hash before running' is pq1's FSBL fingerprint; BitBox adds hardware anti-downgrade in the bootloader, which pq1's rollback floor (OTP) still lacks in approved form. The password-stretching-inside-the-SE pattern could replace or augment pq1's SAES-CMAC KDF if a PIN-derived secret is ever needed.

claim: BitBox disclosed (Aug 2026, Dixence v9.26.5) three firmware flaws found in 'internal AI audits' using 'frontier AI models': a bootloader flaw that let 'an attacker load malicious firmware onto a genuine BitBox02' (precondition: phishing a user into a fake BitBoxApp and unlocking), a memory-corruption bug in the Multi edition exploitable by a hostile host before wallet setup allowing arbitrary code execution, and a silent-payments bug that could lock funds to a wrong address. The Nova 'was never exposed because of its bootloader version'. No evidence of exploitation.
relevance: Two lessons for pq1: the bootloader/FSBL is the one component that cannot be patched after RDP-2 under invariant #10, so it needs the harshest fuzzing/Kani/Miri coverage of its image-verify parser before freeze; and the pre-setup USB path (a device with no wallet yet, talking to a hostile host) must be treated as fully adversarial in pq1's APDU v2 router, not as a bring-up convenience.

claim: Keystone 3 Pro firmware README: 'incorporates three secure elements (Microchip DS28C50, Maxim MAX32520, and Microchip ATECC608A)' and 'Advanced PCI level anti-tamper features'; sensitive data is erased when an attempt to open the enclosure is detected. The MH1903 MCU vendor library 'ships as a pre-compiled blob due to IP restrictions' and secure-element firmware belongs to the vendors, so 'You cannot audit the whole stack line by line'. An Offside Labs-found firmware vulnerability was patched in 1.2.8 (Jan 2024).
relevance: Keystone and GridPlus are the only consumer wallets shipping a PCI-PTS-style active tamper enclosure. pq1's STM32U585 has a TAMP peripheral with active-tamper output/input pairs (TAMP_ATCR) designed for exactly this (pseudo-random pattern over a mesh); pq1 currently uses TAMP only for passive pins with tamp-wipe. A PCB-level mesh over the two SEs and MCU, driven by the active tamper block and backed by the VBAT domain, is the shipped answer to 'can we detect an implant at rest'.

claim: GridPlus Lattice1: a 'Laser Directed Structure (LDS) mesh' around the Secure Compute Environment carries a constant waveform; 'If it's shorted out or the waveform is altered - the device bricks'; the mesh works unplugged on battery 'for around 5 years when unplugged' and '20 years when plugged in'; if the battery dies while armed the device will 'permanently lock and delete all secure data'; the mesh can be disarmed once but never re-armed. The GCE is assumed 'always compromised' and no keys pass through it; 'no factory or engineering debug features that would allow direct access to the SCE'. SafeCards use a PUF and a GridPlus-issued certificate, and uncertified cards are rejected.
relevance: Shows the operational cost of an active mesh (battery, bricking on exhaustion, one-way disarm) that pq1 would have to accept; the VBAT-backed TAMP block on U585 has the same constraints. The GCE/SCE split mirrors pq1's NS/S TrustZone split, and the PUF+vendor-certificate card gating is the same shape as pq1's SE attestation at boot.

claim: Foundation Passport Prime: active tamper detection 'factory resets the device any time it detects that there has been an attempt to remove the screen' or 'tamper with the PCB or chassis in any way' and 'cannot be overridden'; the master seed is split between the SAMA5D2 MPU and the ATECC608C and stored 'XORd with a hash of the user's PIN'; secure boot chain from a hardware root of trust; anti-rollback via firmware timestamps stored in the SE; firmware must be 'signed by 2 out of a possible 4 keys controlled by the Foundation team'; KeyOS is a Rust microkernel that sandboxes each app; QuantumLink BLE 'uses a hybrid scheme combining traditional and post-quantum cryptography' with pairing 'verified via QR code', runs on a separate microcontroller with a hardware kill switch; an onboarding 'software based security check' verifies firmware was not tampered with in transit.
relevance: Three transferable items: (1) 2-of-4 threshold release signing for firmware (pq1's fwsign is a single-key bench flow; a threshold of C10 keys with separately held seeds removes the single-signer insider risk); (2) a display-removal tamper trigger, which is the specific attack on pq1's WYSIWYS anchor (a fake screen is pq1's accepted residual); (3) a hybrid PQ companion link is already shipped by a competitor, so pq1's plaintext USB-HID channel to the companion is a visible gap even if the security argument is 'nothing secret crosses it'.

claim: Cypherock X1 generates seed entropy as the XOR of 256 bits from the ATECC608 TRNG and 256 bits from the STM32L4 TRNG so the result 'stays random even if either chip has a backdoor', then applies Shamir 2-of-5 at the entropy level across the vault (ATECC608A, no NDA) and four EAL6+ NFC cards (proprietary, non-upgradeable applet); the user is 'not required to back up the seed phrase'. The Keylabs audit (Q3 2022) found: exposed test points 'can be utilized to build a programming jig ... as part of a supply chain attack', duplicate ATECC footprints, no potting, and no tamper circuitry; Cypherock replied that for an externally powered device 'any tamper circuitry can be easily spoofed' and that the ultrasonically welded enclosure 'once opened leave visible marks'.
relevance: pq1's XOR split is at rest; Cypherock's is at generation. pq1's seed wizard should XOR OPTIGA TRNG, SE050 TRNG and STM32 TRNG (plus user entropy) so no single vendor's RNG backdoor determines the seed, mirroring pq1's 3-source OptRand. Keylabs' test-point remark applies to pq1's deliberately exposed SWD (required for RDP-0 verification): the first-boot RDP-2 lock is what closes it, and the EVT PCB should carry no other test points on SE buses. Cypherock's 'tamper circuitry is spoofable when externally powered' is the counter-argument to add a VBAT cell if pq1 adopts a mesh.

claim: Keylabs' audit of Cypherock states that 'glitches on chips running at RDP2 of the STM32 family have been known to induce RDP1 behavior, re-enabling the embedded BootROM Bootloader and yielding a device that behaves identically to a chip at RDP1', and recommends STM32 PCROP (execute-only) sectors, noting 'This feature is not set by the Cold Card nor the Trezor T'. Cypherock answered that PCROP 'does not protect read-only data' and that it uses the STM32L4 Firewall enabled by the bootloader instead.
relevance: pq1's invariant #10 rests on RDP-2 freezing option bytes and WRP on the FSBL. The RDP2-to-RDP1 glitch class means the trust story needs defence in depth on STM32U585: enable HDP (hide protection) over the FSBL/secret pages after measurement, keep secrets never in flash plaintext (already true via DHUK wrap), and add the FSBL option-byte read-back tripwire pq1 already has as a runtime detector rather than a prevention. Worth a targeted bench glitch campaign on U585 RDP-2 with the Scaffold setup before the shipping ceremony is approved.

claim: Tangem: 'The private key is generated on-chip during activation and never leaves the card under any circumstances' on a Samsung S3D350A EAL6+ secure element; 'The firmware is factory-installed and non-updatable'; 'Tangem uses a seedless backup model by default' with 2-3 cards sharing one key, a seed phrase being optional; 'Each Tangem card has its own key pair for authenticity verification' and the app 'checks the card's and firmware's authenticity before any wallet operation begins'; audits by Kudelski (2018) and Riscure (2023).
relevance: Tangem is the clearest 'never shows the seed' vendor and the only one that deletes the firmware-update attack surface entirely. pq1's invariant #10 (immutable FSBL + measured slots) is a middle path; the Tangem data point supports offering a 'sealed' production profile where the fw_update NSC commands are compiled out, trading patchability for the elimination of the fwupdate surface in cold-vault deployments.

claim: Satochip (JavaCard applet): the card bricks after a small number of wrong PINs; v0.11 made an ECDH-based secure channel mandatory ('encrypts and authenticates communication between the card and the client'); v0.12 added 'personalisation PKI: allows to verify card authenticity based on a device certificate & PKI' and factory reset; optional 2FA sends each transaction to a second device and 'a one-time code based on the tx hash is sent back to the card for unlocking the signing of the tx', and 2FA is required for message signing, key import and seed reset.
relevance: Tx-hash-bound 2FA from an independent device is a cheap second-approval channel that survives a compromised companion. For pq1 a variant would be: the device shows a short code derived from userOpHash, and a second phone app (or a second pq1) must return a C10 or MAC over it before release. It is a policy-layer complement to clear-signing, like Coldcard's web 2FA.

claim: SeedSigner is 'a verifiably air-gapped, stateless Bitcoin signing device' that 'Temporarily stores seeds in memory while the device is powered; all memory is wiped when power is removed', with the SD card 'removable after boot to ensure no secret data can be written to it', input only via camera QR and output only via screen QR, built from 'inexpensive, publicly available hardware components (usually < $50)' as its supply-chain rationale, with camera/dice entropy and reproducible builds.
relevance: The stateless model is a different point in the design space: no secret at rest means no SE, no PIN counter, and nothing for an implant to exfiltrate at rest. pq1 could offer a stateless 'vault' mode where the seed is loaded per session (SeedQR/NFC share) and the SE halves are never written, for users who prefer backup discipline over device trust; it is also the model that makes pq1's existing NFC/companion attestation irrelevant to the seed.

claim: Krux 'Tamper Check (TC) Flash Hash' (experimental, v24.11.0+): the user sets a TC Code which is combined with the K210 chip's unique ID and stretched with PBKDF2 (100k iterations); the check hashes the TC Code, the device UID and the full flash contents and renders the result as an image plus word sets ('without knowing these three elements, an attacker will not be able to reproduce the TC Flash Hash results'); the firmware region drives the image and first words, the user region the last words. Krux also 'fills empty blocks' of flash with camera-frame entropy so attackers have 'no unused space for malicious code', and any later change to those blocks alters the hash. Limitations: relies on 'running legitimate, uncompromised firmware', and malicious firmware could hash a stored copy from an SD card.
relevance: Two upgrades to pq1's FSBL measurement: (1) measure the whole bank including unused pages, with unused pages filled by random data at first boot and their hash pinned, so an implant or stage-2 payload parked in free flash changes the 8-word fingerprint (today only the active slots are measured); (2) key the displayed fingerprint with a user-chosen secret stretched with the device UID, so a cloned device with the same firmware cannot show the same words. The image rendering is a usability idea for the pixel UI.

claim: Tillitis TKey derives all application keys as cdi = blake2s(UDS, blake2s(device_app), USS): the device 'measures' the app before starting it, 'If the TKey device app is altered in any way the CDI is also changed', 'The same device app loaded onto another TKey results in a different CDI', 'A device app has to be loaded onto the TKey every time you plug it in' and there is 'No persistent storage'; the end-user FPGA configuration and UDS cannot be read out 'even if you break the case and insert it into a programmer board'.
relevance: DICE-style key-binding is the strongest shipped anti-malicious-firmware primitive: if pq1 derived the page-126/DHUK wrap key (or an extra XOR share) from H(UDS, measured secure image), a modified secure image could not unwrap the SE050 BHK or reconstruct entropy even with full MCU compromise, turning the FSBL fingerprint from a human-checked indicator into a cryptographic gate. Cost: every legitimate firmware update becomes a re-wrap migration under the old image, which must be journaled like the first-boot rotation.

claim: ImpedanceVerif (TCHES 2023, Mosavirik/Schaumont/Tajik): on-chip network analyzers characterising the power distribution network impedance 'can detect various classes of tamper events', including attackers who 'place probes in the proximity of the integrated circuits (ICs) package', 'create physical connections between their probes/wires and the system's PCB', 'physically tamper with the PCB's components, chip's package, or substitute the entire PCB', and 'even environment-level tampering activities, such as the proximity of contactless EM probes to the IC package'; the analyzers run 'without any modifications to the system' on commercial FPGA kits, with Wasserstein distance as the detection metric. Silicon Echoes (TCHES 2023) extends this to chip-level Trojans and P&R modifications using injected high-frequency sine waves and scattering parameters on 28 nm FPGAs.
relevance: This is the only published mechanism by which a device could detect an implant, a probe or an EM/laser-FI setup in the field from inside, which is exactly the question behind this research request. A pq1-sized version: at factory, record a PDN frequency-response fingerprint using the U585's ADC/COMP/opamp driven by a TIM-generated stimulus (the consumption-mask timer is a ready stimulus source), store it in the SE, and re-measure at boot and before each sign; a large Wasserstein distance refuses to unlock. It is academic, needs a feasibility study on an MCU rather than an FPGA, but it is the novel anti-implant/anti-SCA-probe idea with real evidence.

claim: Supply-chain tamper evidence as shipped: Coldcard ships 'in a numbered tamper-evident bag' where 'The bag number is recorded on the device at the factory and cannot be changed' and the user verifies the on-screen number against the bag on first power-up; Star Labs' anti-interdiction tiers add 'serialised seals, verification photos, and physical varnish markings', a 'pre-dispatch verification pack' the customer compares on arrival, and a rule that an outer seal broken with official customs tape 'is classed as a routine inspection, not tampering'; Foundation uses tamper-evident packaging plus an onboarding firmware-integrity check.
relevance: pq1's model is verify-before-first-power over SWD, which only experts will do. Layering a factory-burned bag/seal serial in OTP shown by the FSBL on first boot, plus a per-unit pre-dispatch photo pack of PCB and varnish marks, gives ordinary users a transit-tamper check and gives experts a reference image for implant comparison. The customs-tape rule is a useful policy detail for the receipt process.

claim: NGRAVE ZERO: the 'Perfect Key' is generated from chip randomness 'combined with your fingerprint' and the user can 'select groups of 8 characters and shuffle their values', which NGRAVE argues resolves 'any tampering that would have occurred before' (a pre-programmed key); the device claims a 'custom OS that achieved EAL7 certification', 'sensors inside wipe the device if opened' after setup, and QR-only signing with USB-C 'Only for Wall Charging & Secure Firmware Updates'. Coldcard similarly requires 'at least 65 key presses' or 50 dice rolls or 128 coin flips mixed with device entropy. (The widely repeated 'light sensor as entropy' claim appears only in third-party reviews; NGRAVE's own pages list a light sensor in the camera spec without tying it to key generation.)
relevance: User-visible, user-manipulated entropy is the shipped answer to 'what if the TRNG or the factory image is backdoored', and after the Coldcard RNG incident it is the one defence that provably held. pq1's seed wizard should require a dice/coin/key-press entropy phase and show the user that their input changed the words, and the EAL7 marketing is a reminder that pq1's own certification claims must name the evaluated component.

claim: Ledger's Genuine Check is an SE-held factory key plus HSM challenge-response (run on first connection, at each Ledger Wallet access, before app install, before firmware update). Ledger's own threat-model page states it does NOT detect physical hardware modifications such as spying implants when the original Secure Element is intact, cannot verify supply-chain history, and that holographic/anti-tamper seals 'give a false sense of security' because they are easily cloned and packages can be resealed without visible damage.
relevance: Threat: counterfeit or swapped device (supply chain / evil maid). Mechanism: hardware (SE key) + process (HSM). pq1's SE attestation (OPTIGA/SE050 attestation objects at boot) has exactly the same blind spot: an implant on the STM32U585 side or on the LCD/button lines is invisible to any SE-rooted attestation. pq1's ship-at-RDP-0 + SWD verify-before-first-power covers the MCU flash, but not added silicon. Ledger's explicit rejection of seals is a data point against spending on holographic packaging; tamper-evident casing design (see Gen5 finding) is where they went instead.

claim: October 2026 CryptoBilis incident: Ledger stated on X (2026-10-09/10) that it is investigating losses tied to a Southeast-Asian authorized reseller, asked CryptoBilis to pause all sales/shipments, told buyers of the last 90 days not to initiate setup, told already-activated users to move assets to a new signer with a new seed, confirmed that 'one of the impacted users' devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant', said 'we have no indication that Ledger's security infrastructure, systems or services have been compromised', and said it is 'working on further, enhanced anti-tampering solutions'. Mark Karpelès's public description of the implant: a modified Nano X with a concealed board carrying LTE components, an antenna, an eSIM and a microcontroller 'connected to the screen's SPI bus', capturing the recovery phrase as it is displayed during setup; the device passes the Genuine Check. Loss figures ($72M–$93M) are unconfirmed by Ledger.
relevance: Threat: supply-chain hardware implant that taps the display bus and exfiltrates the seed over cellular. Mechanism: Ledger's response is entirely process (reseller halt, re-seed advice, inspection tutorial); no firmware or hardware detection exists. pq1's NV3007 panel sits on SPI1 (PA4/PA5/PA7) and the seed wizard renders the 24 words over that bus — identical exposure class. The only vendor-documented detection is opening the case and comparing against reference photos. This is the strongest argument for pq1 to (a) make the enclosure tamper-evident by design and (b) consider display-bus-level countermeasures (e.g. never rendering the full mnemonic over an unauthenticated bus, or bus-integrity self-checks) rather than relying on attestation. Ledger's statements are secondary-reported (X post not directly fetchable).

claim: Ledger's published hardware-inspection guidance (Nano X User Guide §1.4 'Checking hardware integrity', Ledger-authored PDF): 'The Secure Element checks the full microcontroller flash at boot… If it has been modified, you'll get a warning at boot. As an additional check, you can open the device to verify that no additional chip has been added, compared with the images below, and that the MCU is an STM32WB55 (on revisions 1, 2, 3) and STM32WB35 (on revision 4)', with front/back PCB reference photos per hardware revision; opening voids warranty. The Secure Element attestation can also be verified offline via `python -m ledgerblue.checkGenuineRemote --targetId 0x33000004` against a published secp256k1 batch root-of-trust public key. Ledger's current support article 'Check hardware integrity' (support.ledger.com/article/4404382029329-zd; SPA, not fetchable — content known only from the search snippet) adds Nano Gen5 reference photos and states the Gen5 casing cannot be opened without visible and irreversible damage.
relevance: Threat: added chips / board swap. Mechanism: process (user-performed visual comparison) + hardware (tamper-evident casing on Gen5). Cheap ports for pq1: publish per-revision reference PCB photos and the exact BOM part markings (STM32U585CIU6, OPTIGA, SE050) in the repo, document a user-runnable offline attestation check against a published root, and specify a tamper-evident (destructive-open) enclosure for the production AL_A66 board. Ledger's 2018 35C3 response said the Nano S 'is designed to be easy to open so users can check its integrity'; by Gen5 the design flipped to can't-open-without-damage — a documented shift from inspectability to tamper evidence that pq1 should decide on deliberately.

claim: LSB-002 / Saleem Rashid (2018): the Nano S SE verified the STM32F042 MCU by requesting a dump of its entire flash plus a signature; this was bypassed by code-caving a ~258-byte payload into toolchain intrinsics duplicated between bootloader and firmware (__udivsi3, memcpy, memset) and hooking the dump routine to stream the intact bootloader copy, producing a backdoored all-zero ('abandon') seed and hiding the 'not genuine' warning. Firmware 1.4 countermeasures: MCU code refactored to prevent code caving, signature verification via two different mechanisms, address-fetch randomization, timing constraints so the MCU cannot decompress data on the fly, and CRC fill of unused memory. Ledger claims 'a successful 1.4.1 update is the guarantee that your device has not been tampered with' for the three patched attacks. LSB-005 (wallet.fail, 35C3) later showed the MCU bootloader signature check could be bypassed; Ledger rated it no-impact because the SE still checks the MCU and the MCU holds no PIN/seed.
relevance: Threat: pre-seed supply-chain reflash of the untrusted display/button MCU. Mechanism: firmware (SE-side verification of MCU image). Lesson for pq1 invariant #10: a verifier that reads the verified image *through code the adversary controls* is defeatable; pq1's FSBL reads bank-2 flash directly (good) but its timing-based assumptions and any 'the MCU reports its own contents' pattern (e.g. NS slot measurement via NS-provided pointers) would be the same bug. pq1 cannot make Ledger's 'a successful update proves non-compromise' claim because the measuring root is on the same die — the RDP-0 SWD verify + permanent WRP FSBL is the substitute and should be stated as such.

claim: LSB-013 (Kraken Security Labs, 2020-07-09): JTAG/SWD were left enabled on the Nano X STM32WB55 so advanced users could read flash; consequences were 'Rubber Ducky' reflash into a malicious USB device and a screen-off social-engineering attack, framed by Ledger as supply-chain scenarios; fix in Nano X 1.2.4-2 'checks the integrity of the whole MCU through the Secure Element at each boot, as the Nano S already does' and debug interfaces disabled on newly manufactured devices. Ledger's 'Enhancing the Nano X's security' post says Donjon had identified the risk before Kraken's disclosure.
relevance: Threat: debug-port reflash between factory and first use. Mechanism: hardware (debug lock) + firmware (boot-time MCU integrity). pq1's shipping model deliberately leaves SWD open (RDP-0) until first field boot so that the image can be verified — precisely the window Ledger names as the supply-chain exposure. pq1's mitigation is that the user verifies *before first power*; Ledger's lesson is that a device that is debug-open in transit must have an independent integrity witness at boot, which for pq1 is the WRP-protected FSBL fingerprint — but only after the RDP-2 self-lock has actually run.

claim: LSB-021 (2025-01-10, Guanxing Wen): during MCU firmware update the bootloader accepted a host-supplied `reset_handler` address with no range/alignment/signature validation; pointing it at invalid memory produced an unrecoverable brick and pointing it at attacker code gave code execution at boot. Fix (Nano X 2.4.2, Flex 1.2.2, Stax 1.6.2): the field is strictly validated and the command is part of the signed flow.
relevance: Threat: malicious host during update → permanent DoS or boot-time code execution. Mechanism: firmware. pq1's fw_update BEGIN/CHUNK/COMMIT path must treat every header field that influences control flow (entry/vector address, slot offsets, lengths) as signed and range-checked before COMMIT; a brick-class DoS is itself a reportable finding under Ledger's practice even with funds safe.

claim: CVE-2019-14354 / LSB-006 (Christian Reitter, 2019-08-07): the SSD1306 OLED's per-row power draw is proportional to lit pixels and can be measured via a USB shunt; Ledger reproduced it and could distinguish recovery-phrase words. Firmware 1.6 (2019-11-13) countermeasures: 'randomized screen-update parameters' (contrast, power supply, oscillation frequency continuously randomized), inverted-pixel display of PIN digits and recovery words in boxes, and PIN keypad digit/symbol order randomization. Rated non-critical (CVSS 2.4); Ledger Blue unaffected (LCD); user advice: use a wall charger during setup, Nano X on battery.
relevance: Threat: display-content power side channel during seed display / PIN entry via a hostile cable or power bank. Mechanism: firmware (driver parameter randomization, inverted rendering). pq1's NV3007 TFT has different physics (backlight + SPI write traffic rather than OLED row current), but the seed wizard and PIN entry are the same high-value windows; pq1's consumption mask (TIM PWM, dilution unmeasured per CLAUDE.md) is the analogue and should be validated specifically against display-correlated leakage, and backlight/SPI write-pattern randomization during secret_text rendering is a direct port candidate.

claim: Ledger's 'Secure Screen' claim is internally inconsistent across its own documents: Academy/shop pages say the Stax/Flex/Gen5 E Ink screen 'is controlled directly by the Secure Element chip' and that MCU-driven screens are 'easily hackable'; the Developer Portal hardware-architecture page says the SE 'lacks inputs and outputs', that the STM32WB35 MCU 'acts as the Secure Element's proxy' handling screen/buttons/USB via the SEPROXYHAL protocol and stores no secrets; the 2019 BLE post says 'The Secure Element is in charge of getting user inputs and driving the screen'. The Stax Q&A says the Donjon tested that the SE could 'run this larger screen' but gives no isolation mechanism.
relevance: Threat addressed by the claim: host/MCU malware altering what the user sees. Mechanism: hardware per marketing, firmware-proxied per engineering docs. Falsifiable and relevant to pq1 positioning: no shipping Ledger drives the panel from the SE's own pins — the display path is MCU-proxied in every documented model, which is the same topology as pq1 (S-world on the U585 drives the LCD). The Karpelès implant sat on the display SPI bus regardless of which chip 'controls' it. pq1 should not claim SE-driven display and should document the bus as the residual.

claim: Donjon threat-model 'Transport Security': 'a dedicated, untrusted MCU implements the USB and BLE protocols', forwards decoded packet content to the SE, 'no security assumption is done on the data coming from them', and any increase of the SE's attack surface via transport counts as a threat; a compromised host sending ill-formed USB/BLE packets to get code execution on the MCU is the named risk. BLE pairing on Nano X is ECDH + Numeric Comparison with the code derived via AES-CMAC; when the phone lacks Numeric Comparison the SE warns the user and MITM becomes possible but on-device confirmation is still required.
relevance: Threat: hostile host via USB/BLE. Mechanism: hardware topology (untrusted MCU) + firmware. Maps 1:1 to pq1's NS world (USB HID/APDU router) vs S world: pq1's NSC gateway is the SE channel analogue, and the NS pointer validation + copy-to-S-stack rule is the equivalent of 'no security assumption on transport data'. Worth adopting Ledger's framing explicitly in the pq1 threat model: NS compromise is assumed, and the metric is whether it enlarges the S-world surface.

claim: BOLOS app isolation: apps run in User mode, OS in Supervisor; the SE's ARM MPU maps each app to its own region; apps obtain keys only via a syscall that checks a BIP-32 path allowlist declared in load-time metadata. History: LSB-003 (Volokitin, 2018) — syscalls did not validate pointers/lengths, `cx_hash_sha256` on a NULL pointer acted as a byte-by-byte memory-dump oracle, `cx_rsa_sign`/`cx_ecdsa_sign` returned different errors depending on memory contents (leaking 64 B of the next app), and the 3-wrong-PIN wipe cleared OS data but not app data; fixes in 1.4 added parameter checks, correct MPU windows, and a user-zone wipe that is 'verified at startup'. LSB-014 (2020): the Bitcoin app and most derivatives shipped with an empty OS `--path` restriction so any derivative could sign on Bitcoin's path; fixed by an in-app path lock with a user warning, while the OS-level allowlist was kept empty on purpose to avoid locking users out of nonstandard paths.
relevance: Threat: malicious or buggy app reaching other apps' keys/data. Mechanism: firmware (MPU/syscall gate). pq1 has no third-party apps, so the isolation model does not port, but two bug classes do: (1) gateway error-code diversity as a memory oracle — pq1's NscStatus returns on malformed NS input should be audited so that failure codes never depend on secret memory contents; (2) wipe completeness — pq1's admin-wipe touches pages 123–125 and both SEs; Ledger's 'wipe verified at next boot' is a pattern pq1 should mirror (boot-time assertion that a wipe flag implies all regions are erased).

claim: Donjon PIN threat model: PIN is 4–8 digits, checked at boot before any app is usable; the PIN Try Counter defaults to 3 and exceeding it wipes PIN, seed and secret data, after which the device must be re-initialized; any bypass, guess or extraction of the PIN is in scope. Since firmware 1.6 the PIN keypad order is randomized so an observer counting button clicks (or the 35C3 Blue RF-emanation classifier) cannot infer digits.
relevance: Threat: PIN brute force and PIN-entry observation side channels. Mechanism: firmware/SE. pq1 uses 10 attempts (page 124 + OPTIGA E120 + SE050 UserID) vs Ledger's 3; Ledger's own page quantifies 3 guesses at 0.03% for a uniform 4-digit PIN. pq1's trusted-UI PIN entry on a two-button chord is click-countable; keypad-order randomization in `pin_entry.rs` is a near-free port.

claim: Donjon 'Breaking Trezor One with Side Channel Attacks' (2019-06-17, SSTIC19): a profiled power-analysis attack on Trezor One's digit-by-digit PIN compare — leakage is the difference between stored and presented digit; NICV over 200K traces located points of interest, one LDA classifier per digit trained on an open device, adaptive PIN choice; on 300 PINs the correct digits were always recovered within 10 traces and on average 5.5 attempts, under Trezor's 16-attempt wipe. Power only (EM did not help), ~$1K scope sufficient, scripted with lascar. Disclosed 2018-10-31, fixed by Trezor in trezor-storage 2019-03-06; Donjon did not evaluate the fix.
relevance: Threat: PIN recovery from a stolen device via SCA on a firmware PIN compare. Mechanism: countermeasure shipped as firmware by Trezor; the attack is vendor research. pq1's invariant #2 (PIN compare inside SE silicon, PIN transported under SCP03/Shielded Connection) removes the MCU-side compare entirely — this is a concrete, citable advantage over MCU-only designs. Residual to check: the page-124 precharge and the I2C encryption path must not themselves leak digit-dependent timing/power before the SE compare.

claim: Donjon 'Unfixable Key Extraction Attack on Trezor' (2019-07-01): physical seed extraction from Trezor One/T, KeepKey, B Wallet and clones with ~$100 of hardware in ~5 minutes (3 min prep + 2 min extraction), all firmware versions, PIN brute-force adds minutes; unfixable without hardware redesign so details were withheld; disclosed to Trezor Dec 2018, no bounty; vendors' response was to exclude physical attacks from the threat model or use a passphrase, for which Ledger recommends ~37 random characters to match 24-word strength. Donjon's seed-confidentiality page cites glitch attacks, SRAM seed extraction and EMFI as the demonstrated extraction classes.
relevance: Threat: physical seed extraction from a stolen MCU-only wallet. Mechanism: hardware (SE storage) is Ledger's answer. pq1's dual-SE XOR split keeps the at-rest seed off the U585, but pq1 reconstructs the full entropy in S-SRAM for the 120 s signing window — exactly the SRAM-extraction state Donjon's work targets. The design implication is to minimise the reconstructed-entropy residency (derive what is needed, zeroize early) and to treat voltage/EM glitching of the U585 during the unlocked window as in-scope, since the U585 is not a CC-evaluated part.

claim: Ledger Donjon ships Rainbow (open-source Unicorn-based side-channel and fault-injection simulator, since 2019) with fault models `fault_skip` (instruction skip) and `fault_stuck_at` (destination register forced to 0s/1s), and `fi_check`, a Rust-oriented CI/IDE tool that faults every instruction in turn and reports any run where a function returns `true` without crashing, mapping hits to source via addr2line. Worked example: an imperative Cortex-M3 PIN compare was vulnerable to bit-set; a functional one had 9 vulnerable points, a protected Boolean type reduced it to 2 (an early size check), then 0. Limits stated by Ledger: cannot find unmodelled effects.
relevance: Threat: single-fault bypass of security decisions. Mechanism: process/tooling (vendor-shipped). pq1 already has the `rainbow` skill and FI sentinels (CfiCounter, Hamming-distant constants, double-compute in c10_sign_verified); a CI fault-sweep over the secure image's decision points (gated_unlock, confirm(), fw_update verify, the chord-arming gate) in the style of fi_check would turn the FI story from 'countermeasures present' into 'countermeasures measured', and is cheaper than the open hardware-FI gates (EF-swarm F15).

claim: Scaffold (Ledger Donjon) is an open-hardware, LGPLv3 FPGA motherboard for IC security evaluation: USB-controlled Python API, clock glitching, four 5 V pulse outputs compatible with ALPhANOV PDM laser sources, four 10 ns-resolution delay/pulse generators with chaining, and an 11x power-measurement amplifier; all fabrication files are published. Donjon's SiliconToaster EMFI tool is described as injecting pulses up to 1 kV.
relevance: Threat: lab-grade FI/SCA against the device. Mechanism: process (vendor evaluation tooling). pq1's bench (tools/bench, Scaffold + Rigol validated per memory) already uses this exact board; the open items are the crowbar glitcher and Scaffold↔U585 coupling. Ledger's tooling being open means pq1 can publish reproducible FI/SCA campaign scripts as evidence — something Ledger itself does not publish for its own devices.

claim: Donjon physical-resistance and RNG threat-model pages: adversary has physical access and 'high potential (expertise, time, equipment)'; in-scope attacks are laser and EM, glitch FI, power/EM side channels and hardware reverse engineering; Ledger relies on a Secure Element plus software built for these attacks. The SE TRNG is evaluated to EAL5+/AIS-31 by a third-party lab across temperature, frequency and voltage with a mathematical randomness proof, and any undetected entropy reduction counts as a valid attack. Ledger's Academy page claims the SE has 'light detectors for laser fault injection', temperature sensors, voltage-glitch detectors and 'complex countermeasures to hide its electromagnetic radiation and power usage'.
relevance: Threat: lab physical attacks and RNG weakness. Mechanism: hardware (certified SE). pq1's long-term secret halves live in two CC-certified SEs but pq1's OS, crypto (SPHINCS+C10) and TRNG run on the STM32U585, which has no CC/AIS-31 evaluation; pq1 should state that its seed-generation TRNG is the U585 RNG (optionally mixed with SE TRNG output) and consider sourcing seed entropy from the SEs' AIS-31 TRNGs as well, which would let pq1 cite the same certification Ledger does for the entropy source.

claim: Secure Element certification facts: Ledger Stax/Flex/Gen5/Nano S Plus use ST33K1M5 (Cortex-M35P), Common Criteria EAL6+ (ALC_FLR.1) under NSCIB certificate NSCIB-CC-0428014-CR2, valid 2022-08-17 to 2027-08-17; Nano X uses ST33J2M0 (EAL5+). ST's May 2026 ST33K1M5 data brief (Rev 5) lists an optional certified PQC library (NesLib-PQML, ML-KEM and ML-DSA). Ledger's own Academy page assigns EAL5+ to Nano X and EAL6+ to Nano S Plus and Stax.
relevance: Threat: chip-level physical attack. Mechanism: hardware. pq1's OPTIGA Trust M V3 and SE050 are both EAL6+ class parts, so the chip-level claim is at parity; the difference is that Ledger's OS and signing execute inside the certified boundary while pq1's SPHINCS+ signing executes on the uncertified U585. Note that ST now offers an in-SE ML-DSA library — the first vendor path to PQ signing inside a certified SE — which is a competitive datapoint even though pq1's SPHINCS+C10-only invariant (#5) rules out ML-DSA.

claim: Ledger firmware delivery and secure channel: firmware upgrades 'are signed and sent through a secure channel from the HSM to the Secure Element itself' providing attestation, encryption and MAC, and Ledger states firmware confidentiality 'is not a basis of the device's security'. Channel history: LSB-001 (2018, Isnard) — the SCP-02-inspired channel omitted the MAC and status 0x6802 gave a padding oracle (few bytes recovered, fixed by adding the MAC in 1.4.1 plus server-side mitigations); LSB-016 (2021, Isnard) — CBC-MAC on variable-length messages with a 14-byte truncated tag allowed length-extension forgery at 2^15 effort and a padding oracle decrypting one block in hours; fixed in Nano S 2.0.0 / Nano X 1.3.0 with constant-time full padding checks and immediate channel teardown on error, with a new protocol planned.
relevance: Threat: MITM/forgery on the SE↔HSM update channel. Mechanism: firmware (SCP).
