Two direct checks for pq1's SE tunnels: OPTIGA Shielded Connection uses AES-128-CCM-8 — an 8-byte tag, shorter than the 14-byte tag Ledger found inadequate under length-extension (CCM is not CBC-MAC-extendable, but the tag-truncation forgery bound 2^-64 per attempt should be stated in HARDENING.md), and both tunnels must close on the first MAC/padding error rather than retry. Ledger's explicit 'firmware confidentiality is not a security basis' matches pq1's signed-not-encrypted fw_update stance.

claim: LSB-023 (2026-08-27): a TOCTOU (CWE-362) in the Ledger Secure SDK's command path — a host could send a new APDU while the app was awaiting on-screen approval, overwriting signing parameters held in global state (e.g. the derivation path) after display but before signature; each app had been individually responsible for rejecting interleaved commands. Regression introduced August 2025; Ethereum app 1.22.2 (2026-08-13) added per-app guards; SDK v26.6.1 (2026-08-21) rejects interleaved commands centrally before application code; first-party apps rebuilt and republished the same day. Found by Ledger's internal review; OneKey later demonstrated it against 1.22.1.
relevance: Threat: compromised host mutating a request during user review. Mechanism: firmware (dispatcher-level state guard). pq1's sign handlers copy NS buffers to S-stack before parse and run confirm() in S-world, which structurally prevents the overwrite, but the pq1 NSC dispatcher should be audited for reentrancy: no NSC call (including LOCK, IS_UNLOCKED, FW_*) may be serviced while a confirm dialog is pending, and the rejection must live in `nsc/mod.rs`, not in each cmd_* handler — Ledger's lesson is that per-handler guards decay.

claim: LSB-024 (2026-08-27, Felipe Manzano/Bitfinding, variant by Florian Pradines; rated High): the Ethereum app's Generic Transaction Parser counted array entries with a 16-bit value but stored the count in an 8-bit countdown, so a 257-element array was recorded as 1 and only the final element was clear-signed while the signature covered the whole batch; requires only a compromised host and a descriptor iterating an attacker-controlled array >255; affected 1.19.0–1.22.2; fixed in 1.22.3 (2026-08-25) by rejecting counts that do not fit. Timeline shows the fix was merged 2026-05-05 but 1.22.2 was tagged without it on 2026-08-13 and the reporter had to flag the omission.
relevance: Threat: clear-signing bypass by integer narrowing in the descriptor-driven renderer. Mechanism: firmware. pq1's multiSend cap (≤6 records, exact framing, page-budget overflow refuses) and ERC-7730 renderer are the analogous code; every count/length that is narrowed between parser and renderer must refuse rather than wrap (a Kani harness for 'rendered element count == signed element count' is the right shape). Second lesson is release provenance: a merged fix missing from the tagged build — pq1's reproducible-build + release manifest gates should assert the fix commit is an ancestor of the tag.

claim: LSB-025 (2026-08-27, Ledger internal automated review; CWE-285): in the swap flow, which does not prompt the user on-device, the Ethereum app validated only the destination address and amount, so an ERC-20 `approve` (same field layout as `transfer`) with the deposit address and amount passed as a payment, granting the provider's deposit address an allowance instead of paying; appended calldata was also accepted. Affected 1.20.0–1.22.2; fixed in 1.22.3 by checking the operation type first, rejecting appended data, then comparing address/amount.
relevance: Threat: operation-type confusion in a no-prompt signing path. Mechanism: firmware. pq1 has no silent-sign flows (every release goes through confirm), which is the structural fix; the portable checks are (a) ERC-20 decoding keys on selector before argument shape (pq1's `tx/src/selectors` does this — worth a negative test for `approve` vs `transfer` with identical args) and (b) exact-length calldata framing with trailing bytes refused, which pq1 already enforces for multiSend records and should enforce for every known-shape decoder.

claim: Companion-side parsing failures that reached the signer: LSB-015 (2021-01-13) — Ethereum app 1.6.0 regression stopped displaying contract data even with 'Contract data' enabled, so an alternate client could obtain a signature on undisplayed data (fixed 1.6.4); LSB-020 (2023-11-20, Ian Fisher) — `@ledgerhq/hw-app-eth` used Node `Buffer.from` on odd-length hex so an EIP-712 uint256 `0x123` became `0x12` and the device displayed the hash of the altered message (fixed in hw-app-eth 6.34.7 / Ledger Live 2.70.0); Ledger's mitigation advice was to compare the hash shown by Live with the hash on the device.
relevance: Threat: companion/library altering the signed payload. Mechanism: firmware (device-side decode) and process (hash cross-check). pq1's design decision to decode EIP-712 (Safe, CoW) and ERC-20 on-device from raw bytes, with the companion unable to substitute a hash, is exactly the countermeasure these two bulletins motivate; the RAW32 'show the full hash' fallback mirrors Ledger's cross-check advice and its weakness (a user must compare 64 hex characters).

claim: LSB-022 (2026-06-04, internal review): the Monero app's `INS_GET_CHACHA8_PREKEY` returned the full 200-byte Keccak state after one Keccak-f over (view key ‖ spend key ‖ padding) in a single block from a zero state; since Keccak-f is public and invertible this revealed both secret keys to any host able to send APDUs to an unlocked device with the app open, with no user confirmation. Fixed in Monero app 2.1.4 using SHAKE256 with a proper squeeze, a domain-separation label, only the view key as input, and explicit clearing of intermediate buffers.
relevance: Threat: a gateway command that returns an intermediate cryptographic state becomes a key-extraction oracle. Mechanism: firmware. pq1 invariant #4 says NSC returns only opaque non-secret data; this bulletin is the audit template: enumerate every CMD_* output (OFFCHAIN_STATUS counters, GET_INIT_CODE, GET_WALLET_ADDRESS, FW_STATUS, GET_REMAINING) and prove each is a function of public inputs or a properly squeezed/derived value, never raw permutation or hash state.

claim: Clear Signing lineage per Ledger: Ethereum plugins in 2021 (device-specific code per integration), then a Generic Parser driven by structured metadata, the Clear Signing Initiative in 2024, ERC-7730 v1 released 2025, and on 2026-05-15 Ledger transferred governance of the ERC-7730 registry to the Ethereum Foundation alongside ERC-7730 v2 (cross-chain, software-wallet compatible, ERC-4626 expressiveness) developed with WalletConnect, Fireblocks, Sourcify, Trezor and Cyfrin; the registry is github.com/ethereum/clear-signing-erc7730-registry stewarded by the EF Trillion Dollar Security Initiative, and Ledger open-sourced a Linter, Tester, LLM-based Analyzer and Generator. Sourcify's docs state that registry inclusion 'does not mean that a descriptor is safe or approved'.
relevance: Threat: blind signing. Mechanism: process (registry) + firmware (parser). pq1's pinned `ERC7730_DESCRIPTORS_ROOT` built by dbgen from the upstream registry matches this model; the actionable differences are that Ledger's descriptors are delivered at runtime via a signed metadata channel while pq1 compiles a Merkle root into firmware (stronger provenance, slower updates), and that pq1 should track ERC-7730 v2 since the registry governance has moved and v1-only parsers will fall behind the corpus.

claim: ERC-8176 (draft, created 2026-02-26, author Bartosz Rozwarski; requires EIP-712/1271/7730) defines an EAS schema `bytes32 descriptorHash` (UID 0xe023eef1…b5c2, resolver = zero address so anyone may attest, revocable) on mainnet EAS 0xA1207F3BBa224E2c9c3c6D5aF63D0eb1582Ce587; the hash is Keccak-256 over the RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization of the fully include-resolved descriptor; wallets must recompute the hash, check expiry, recover the attester (ECDSA or ERC-1271), check revocation against the canonical EAS contract and apply their own attester trust-set/threshold. Security considerations state it does not protect against malicious attesters, attester key compromise, semantic errors in descriptors or compromised signing pipelines.
relevance: Threat: descriptor tampering/substitution in transit. Mechanism: process (attestations) consumed by firmware policy. pq1's stance that ERC-8176 is catalogue-admission only (host dbgen verifies the secp256k1 EAS attestations; firmware grants no runtime authority) is consistent with the ERC's own trust model and with invariant #5; the falsifiable implementation detail to pin in dbgen is the JCS+Keccak descriptor-hash recipe and the schema UID.

claim: Ledger Recover (white paper, 2023-06-21, repo archived 2024-08-01): the 256-bit BIP-39 entropy (not the PBKDF2 seed) is encrypted with AES-256-CBC 'using a key common to all devices', then split with Pedersen verifiable secret sharing over secp384r1 into a 2-of-3 scheme across Coincover (UK), EscrowTech (US) and Ledger (FR) HSMs (Thales ProtectServer, FIPS 140-2 L3); each share is sent over an ephemeral ECDH (secp256k1) channel to an HSM authenticated by a Ledger-signed certificate, with the device authenticated by its production certificate; Ledger is the root of trust for backup-provider and orchestrator HSM certificates; the user confirms on-device before shares are exported; identity verification is 1 IDV at backup and 1 independent IDV per provider at restore; a one-time security code is derived from the ECDH MAC/ENC keys; share deletion is a separate flow.
relevance: Threat: user loses all devices/backups. Mechanism: firmware (OS seed-export path) + process (IDV, custodial HSMs). Its existence is the critical datapoint for pq1: once the OS has a consented seed-export primitive, device attestation plus on-screen consent become the only barrier to exfiltration, and a fleet-wide 'key common to all devices' is a single point of failure. pq1's invariants #1/#4 (no full entropy on one chip, no seed leaves TrustZone) mean the equivalent capability is structurally absent — a defensible differentiator to state explicitly rather than implicitly.

claim: Donjon threat-model 'Secure Display and Inputs' states the property as 'What you see is what you sign', delivered 'through the genuineness property, the firmware integrity mechanism, and the device architecture', with host malware altering displayed content or injecting keystrokes, non-legitimate SE firmware, arbitrary code controlling the display, and input bypass as the named threats; 'User Consent' states 'user approval is always required for signing transactions and messages' to prevent use as a 'signing black box'. Neither page names which chip drives the screen, defines blind-signing policy, or lists residual risks.
relevance: Threat: WYSIWYS violation. Mechanism: composite (attestation + firmware integrity + topology). pq1 can go further in writing than Ledger does: name the display bus, name the FSBL-measured atlas (ui-px re-hash before/after every dialog), name scroll-to-end arming, and name the residuals (display-bus implant, post-boot fake screen) — Ledger's public model leaves all of these unstated, which is a gap pq1's documentation can exploit for credibility.

claim: Trezor's STM32U5 boot chain is boardloader (immutable, WRP-protected, 'hardware root of trust') -> bootloader (updatable; 'the last stage with access to the flash secrets area') -> secmon (secure-privileged, verified by bootloader with a 2-of-3 Ed25519 CoSi key set; does NOT re-verify the kernel) -> kernel (non-secure privileged) -> coreapp (non-secure unprivileged). Secmon exposes a limited smcall API whose verifiers validate arguments; MPU/SAU/GTZC enforce non-overlapping regions; any violation -> MemFault -> RSOD -> reset. Flash secrets are hidden with HDP 'until the next reset'. Trezor's own doc concedes 'coreapp can request raw secrets and receive them, and that the separation of layers is still being improved' (SMCALL_STORAGE_GET returns raw storage entries to NS).
relevance: pq1 invariant #4 (no secrets in NS, ever) is strictly stronger than what Trezor Safe 5/7 ship today. Two levers pq1 does not use: (a) STM32U5 HDP (secure hide-protection) to make the secret pages unreadable even to secure code after the FSBL/first-boot stage — pq1 keeps pages 123-127 readable by the whole S-world runtime; (b) a formal per-smcall argument-verifier layer (pq1 has NsPtr validation but no per-command verifier table). Also note Trezor's bootloader verifies secmon separately from the NS firmware — pq1's FSBL measures both slots as one unit.

claim: Trezor Safe 7's post-quantum signing covers ONLY the boardloader->bootloader step, and is hybrid: the boot header carries up to 3 SLH-DSA signatures (parameter set 'sphincs-sha2-128s', PARAMS define in core/embed/crypto/build.rs:320; BOOT_HEADER_PQ_SIGNATURE_LEN = 7856) over a Merkle root of the bootloader code, plus Ed25519 signatures over SHA-256(merkle_root || slh_signature). The code verifies Ed25519 FIRST ('do it before we verify the PQC signature'), then SLH-DSA; both must pass. Trezor's rationale: 'if SLH-DSA were flawed before quantum computers matter, exploitation would still require a valid EdDSA signature.' Bootloader->secmon/firmware verification remains pure Ed25519 CoSi (image.c check_image_header_sig), and Trezor states 'Trezor Safe 7 can run post-quantum updates, but these updates don't exist yet.'
relevance: pq1 is C10-only for firmware update (invariant #5, no classical fallback) — the opposite of Trezor's hybrid. Falsifiable comparison point for the README/threat model: pq1 should state explicitly why it rejects hybrid (single primitive, one verifier) and that its PQ coverage is end-to-end (FSBL measure + fw_update verify), whereas Trezor's PQ coverage is boardloader->bootloader only. Trezor's Merkle-root-over-code + proof structure (allows a signed header to cover multiple images) is a packaging idea for pq1's manifest v6.

claim: Trezor Safe 7 device authentication (Suite, 'May 2026 updates'; trezorctl support added 2026-03-18 commit 82ca4a0f37; firmware changelog #6807 'Added MCU device attestation with ML-DSA-44') uses three per-chip certificates: OPTIGA Trust M (ECDSA secp256r1), TROPIC01 (Ed25519), STM32U5 MCU (ML-DSA-44, cert stored in the HDP-hidden secret area, private key regenerated on each sign from a seed via secret_key_mcu_device_auth() -> mldsa_keypair_internal(), then memzero'd). The challenge is prefixed 'AuthenticateDevice:' with compact-size framing. Trezor says the certificate is 'checked only by Trezor Suite and then immediately discarded.'
relevance: pq1 has no device-authenticity attestation at all (its post-sale trust story is RDP-0 SWD verification before first power + boot fingerprint). A C10-signed MCU attestation keyed from a DHUK/BHK-derived seed (per-die, never stored) would be a one-primitive analogue of Trezor's ML-DSA-44 MCU cert, and both SEs already have attestation objects (OPTIGA E0E0-E0E3 certs; SE050 attestation). Note the MCU-key-from-seed pattern: regenerate from a hardware-rooted seed per use, never persist the expanded key.

claim: Trezor security portal, 'Reported on August 16, 2026', 'Reported by Anonymous', 'Reward 1350 USD': 'Trezor Safe 7 authenticity proofs were verified against a combined key set rather than per secure element' so that 'a single valid proof could satisfy all three checks.' Fix: 'Each proof is now bound to its own element.'
relevance: Direct design rule for any pq1 multi-chip attestation (OPTIGA + SE050 + MCU): the verifier must bind each proof to that element's own root-key set and reject a proof that satisfies another element's slot; otherwise one compromised/cloned element's proof (e.g. a TROPIC01-class LFI-extracted key) satisfies the whole check. Also a reminder that host-side verifier logic (Suite/trezorlib) is part of the TCB for attestation.

claim: Ledger Donjon (published 2025-03-12; reported to Trezor 2024-11-12) bypassed Trezor Safe 3's supply-chain countermeasures: the MCU is a 'TRZ32F429' ('electrically an STM32F429 in a custom package'); step 1 voltage-glitch the RDP level fetch at boot to downgrade RDP2->RDP1; step 2 in RDP1 reprogram config via debug; step 3 glitch the BootROM READ_MEMORY RDP check (256 B per glitch). The Optiga attestation key only signs 'if the microcontroller proves it knows' a per-device pre-shared secret 'stored in the microcontroller's flash' in '32 contiguous bytes, so a single successful READ_MEMORY glitch is enough'; Donjon calls this link 'somewhat weak' because it 'proves access to a secret, not the software running on the microcontroller.' The Suite firmware-hash check was 'fully bypass[ed]'. Impact: reprogrammed MCU with 'the full impression of an authentic device', e.g. bias seed entropy (PR #4155) or ECDSA nonces (#2637). Trezor: no firmware fix for Safe 3 ('Hi, unfortunately not'); Safe 5 unaffected because it 'uses a more recent microcontroller'.
relevance: pq1's OPTIGA PBS (E140) and SE050 SCP03 keys are likewise MCU-held secrets that prove possession, not measured code. The rdp2-self-lock design rotates them to DHUK/BHK-derived values, which defeats a flash DUMP (per-die keys) but NOT code execution on the die after an RDP downgrade (any code on the die can recompute DHUK-derived keys). Consequence: pq1's implant/supply-chain story must not rest on SE pairing-secret possession; the FSBL fingerprint + RDP-0 pre-power verification is the right anchor, and a future SE-bound attestation should be bound to a firmware measurement (e.g. OPTIGA/SE050 object released only after the FSBL writes a measurement-derived value the SE compares), not to a static pairing secret.

claim: Kraken Security Labs (2020-01-31; discovered 2019-10-30): on STM32F205 (Trezor One) and STM32F427 (Model T), voltage glitch ~170 us into BootROM re-enables JTAG/SWD, ~180 us re-enables the BootROM bootloader (RDP2->RDP1), then a second glitch on the Read Memory RDP check dumps flash 256 B at a time; '15 minutes of physical access'; setup 'several hundred dollars', mass-producible '$75'; 4-digit PIN brute-forced in <2 min at ~85 H/s. Trezor's 2020 response: passphrase mitigates; a real fix 'would require a hardware redesign'. Unciphered re-demonstrated the same class on a Trezor T in May 2023 and Trezor characterised it as 'an RDP downgrade attack' it 'can't fix with firmware'.
relevance: Baseline threat for any STM32: pq1 must assume an RDP-2 -> RDP-1/RDP-0 downgrade is a reachable adversary capability on U585 until proven otherwise, which is why the dual-SE XOR split (no seed bit on the MCU) and SE-silicon PIN compare matter more than MCU-side hardening. Also supports keeping PBKDF2-class stretching off the MCU alone (Trezor's 85 H/s PIN brute force).

claim: Trezor's STM32U5 production option-byte profile (option_bytes.c): RDP level 2, WRP1AR covering the boardloader pages, TZEN, nBOOT0, SECBOOTADD0 = boardloader start | BOOT_LOCK, SECWM secure watermarks for both banks, HDP1 ending at the secret sector (HDP1EN), and the four OEM RDP-regression key registers explicitly written to 0xFFFFFFFF 'to ensure that there is no ability to reverse the RDP', with option_bytes_check_oem_keys() asserting FLASH->NSSR OEM1LOCK/OEM2LOCK are clear ('OEM1 KEY SET' is fatal). The boardloader re-checks the full option-byte set on EVERY boot; a mismatch 'may indicate a first boot after manufacturing, or a potential hardware fault or exploit attempt' and triggers secret_safety_erase() (regenerates BHK, erases storage) before resetting.
relevance: Two concrete gaps vs pq1's first-boot RDP-2 self-lock + FSBL tz-1 tripwire: (1) pq1's design docs never mention the U5 OEM1/OEM2 RDP-regression keys — if a factory or attacker provisions an OEM key, RDP-2 becomes reversible to RDP-1 with password; the self-lock ceremony must write 0xFFFFFFFF and assert OEMxLOCK clear, and the tz-1 tripwire should check NSSR lock bits; (2) Trezor's response to an option-byte mismatch is a secret wipe, whereas pq1's tripwire 'reads only, halts on a persistent mismatch' — a halt leaves secrets in place for a second attempt. Note Trezor keeps HDP over the secret sector so the secret pages become invisible after the boot stage.

claim: Trezor's STM32U5 TAMP configuration enables internal tampers ITAMP1 (backup-domain voltage), ITAMP2 (temperature), ITAMP3 (LSE CSS), ITAMP5 (RTC overflow), ITAMP6 ('JTAG/SWD access when RDP > 0'), ITAMP7/12/13 (ADC4 analog watchdog monitoring 1-3), ITAMP8 (monotonic counter overflow), ITAMP9 ('Crypto peripherals fault (SAES, AES, PKA, TRNG)'), ITAMP11 (IWDG reset while tamper flag set), plus external TAMP2; a tamper 'erases part of RAM' (backup registers incl. BHK) and the device shows RSOD with reason 'VOLTAGE'/'TEMPERATURE'/etc. The BHK is loaded into TAMP backup registers and locked (TAMP_SECCFGR_BHKLOCK) so it is 'non-readable and usable only through the SAES peripheral'; on 'WF_ERROR_FATAL' (bootloader saw secbools 'randomly flip, most likely due to glitch') it regenerates the BHK and erases storage.
relevance: pq1's `tamp` feature is described as a Trezor port that is 'log-only by itself' with `tamp-wipe` forced on for shipping, and GTZC2/TAMP securing is still an open follow-up. Audit items: confirm pq1 enables ITAMP6 (debug access = glitch/RDP-downgrade detector), ITAMP9 (crypto-peripheral fault = FI detector around SAES/TRNG), the ADC4 analog watchdogs on VDD (a cheap in-silicon voltage-glitch detector), and that a tamper event zeroizes the BHK register (pq1 page 126 wraps the SE050 BHK) rather than only logging. Trezor's 'secbool flipped -> regenerate BHK + wipe' policy is a shipped example of fault-detected-implies-wipe.

claim: Trezor's fault-injection software countermeasures, as shipped: (a) random_delays.c runs a ChaCha-DRBG (TRNG-seeded) and a 1 ms periodic 'RDI' interrupt that busy-waits a random 0-255 + per-session jitter on every tick, plus wait_random() whose loop keeps an i+j==wait invariant and double-checks completion, else error_shutdown('(glitch)'); (b) boardloader commit ad0ee485c9 (2025-07-09, 'add simple fih measures') inserts fih_delay() = systick_delay_us(rng_get() % 128) before every security-relevant ensure() ('fih_ensure'); (c) the bootloader keeps firmware_present and firmware_present_backup, compares them under a volatile dont_optimize_out_true, and jumps through a volatile function pointer that defaults to failed_jump_to_firmware() -> error_shutdown('(glitch)'); (d) the boardloader's next_stage_addr is a volatile 'FIH' variable set only at the end of ensure_signed_bootloader(). An older bootloader antiglitch.c was removed 2025-06-10 as 'obsolete'. Secmon exposes wait_random / random_delays_* to the kernel.
relevance: pq1 has stronger per-signature FI hardening (double-compute + compare + verify-before-release, CfiCounter, Hamming-distant sentinels) but no continuous timing desynchronisation: no RDI-style background jitter interrupt, and the FSBL does fixed-timing verification which makes glitch windows (e.g. the c10 verify compare, the fingerprint render) predictable. Cheap levers: random pre-check delay before each FSBL `ensure`, duplicate-and-compare of the slot-valid secbool, default-fail function pointer for the slot branch, and a secure-world periodic jitter timer (pq1 already owns a S-only TIM for the idle timeout).

claim: Trezor's consumption mask on STM32U5 drives TIM2 CH1 PWM on PA5 with a circular GPDMA linked list of 119 random CCR values (TIMER_PERIOD 16000 at 160 MHz, ~10 kHz), DMA channel marked SEC|PRIV with secure source/destination, re-randomised by consumption_mask_randomize() with rng_get(); it drives no explicit external load in the driver.
relevance: pq1's consumption-mask port is the same mechanism (TIM2/TIM3 CH1, randomised duty) and CLAUDE.md already records that its dilution is unmeasured on both boards. Trezor's implementation differs in using a DMA-fed 119-sample random sequence (no CPU involvement, so the mask does not itself modulate with secret-dependent code) — pq1's `randomize()` must be called by the caller. Neither vendor publishes a measured SNR reduction; a pq1 measurement with the bench tooling (tools/bench, scared/lascar) would be a genuine differentiator.

claim: Trezor Safe 3/5 Optiga PIN protection (docs/core/misc/optiga.md): the KEK derivation chains Optiga operations where every step is wrapped as digest = HMAC(stretched_pin, ''); out = optiga_op(digest); stretched_pin = HMAC(stretched_pin, out), so that 'even if the communication link or the Optiga is completely compromised, possibly even malicious, it will not reduce the security of the Trezor any more than if the Optiga was not integrated'. Steps: 2x (AES-CMAC with PIN_CMAC E200 + ECDH with hash-to-curve on PIN_ECDH E0F3), then HMAC with PIN_HMAC F1D8, then AutoRef auth on STRETCHED_PIN F1D4 to read PIN_SECRET F1D0. Counters: STRETCHED_PIN_CTR E120 (16), PIN_HMAC_CTR E122 (16), and a lifetime PIN_TOTAL_CTR E121 'Limit set to 600000, meaning 150000 unlock attempts'. 'An attacker would need to be able to extract each of the secrets in PIN_CMAC, PIN_ECDH, PIN_HMAC and PIN_SECRET to conduct an offline brute-force search'. A dedicated 'PIN-only attack' (same PIN on two devices) mitigation requires PIN_HMAC_CTR writes be authorised by STRETCHED_PIN. The MCU additionally runs PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 10000 iterations (20000 total) 'to thwart brute-force attacks in case the attacker is able to circumvent the PIN entry counter mechanism'.
relevance: pq1 uses OPTIGA E120 LUC + F1D0 AutoRef and SE050 UserID for PIN gating, but the dual-SE unlock releases XOR halves rather than stretching a KEK. Levers worth porting: (1) wrap every SE-returned value in an MCU-side HMAC chain so a hostile/compromised OPTIGA or a tapped I2C bus cannot weaken below the no-SE baseline (pq1's tunnels are the current answer; this is defence-in-depth against the Grover-2^64 residual accepted in invariant #3); (2) a lifetime PIN_TOTAL_CTR-style counter bounding total stretching operations (anti-extraction oracle) — pq1's E120 32-lifetime cap is the same idea only for failures; (3) spread the secret over several OPTIGA object types (CMAC key, ECDH key, PRESSEC, AUTOREF) so a single-object-type extraction bug is insufficient — pq1 keeps half_O in one data object F1D1.

claim: Trezor Safe 7 PIN flow (vendor doc): the MCU combines the PIN with 'a random salt held in its own flash memory'; TROPIC01 'mixes in its own secret and returns a transformed value' using the MAC-and-Destroy hardware block, where each check 'consumes a one-time physical slot inside the chip' (firmware: 64 slots x 32 B per privilege level, 'wear leveling of mac-and-destroy slots' #6136); OPTIGA 'verifies the value and, if correct, contributes its final secret piece' under 'a non-resettable counter'; the decryption key 'exists only for a moment in memory and is never stored'; the MCU 'enforces no attempt limits of its own' and 'cannot override chip-level protections'; the wallet backup is encrypted in MCU flash, not on either SE; after 10 wrong PINs the wallet is erased. Per Donjon, MACANDD keys 'come from OTP fuses and a PUF' and reference data sits 'in a flash partition behind a hardware firewall' with 'no direct [CPU] access'.
relevance: Architectural contrast for pq1's three-way attempt consumption (MCU page 124 + OPTIGA E120 + SE050 UserID): Trezor deliberately has NO MCU-side counter, treating the MCU as untrusted for rate limiting; pq1's page-124 precharge is a conservative extra. pq1's XOR split (neither SE alone reveals any bit) is strictly stronger than Trezor's 'SE holds the key to decrypt a backup in MCU flash' because a Safe 7 whose MCU is dumped plus one SE compromised still needs the other SE — same as pq1 — but Trezor's claim 'cannot override chip-level protections' was weakened by the TROPIC01 MACANDD compromise below.

claim: TROPIC01 laser fault injection (Ledger Donjon, published 2026-06-03; project start 2025-12-23, first success 2026-01-26, disclosed 2026-01-27; Tropic Square advisory ODR_TR01_SA_2026012900_1v0, CVSS 3.1 5.7 Medium, 'all production versions of TROPIC01 in the field are affected'): a single 1064 nm pulse (~5 um spot, Alphanov PDM+) through the package backside 'without thinning the die', timed to 'the last ~10 us of the verification window' of the SPECT coprocessor's RFC 8032 Ed25519 final R==Q comparison, bypasses signature verification; two faults are needed (one during update, one at boot), ~1 h each without trace synchronisation, boot fault 'near 90%' with retries; faults worked on a subset of positions 'with laser detectors enabled' and 'without ever triggering an alarm'. Result: arbitrary non-persistent firmware on the SE (must be redone each power cycle). After Tropic Square found a MACANDD path, Donjon found vulnerabilities that combined 'completely compromise the MACANDD mechanism' from arbitrary firmware. Field mitigation: disable MAINTENANCE mode in R-config (raises bar; combined attack still 'consistently in under an hour'); hardened silicon 'late 2026'; full report 'spring 2027'. Trezor: cannot create tampered devices (non-persistent), PIN/funds/backup not exposed because Optiga + STM32U5 remain.
relevance: Validates pq1's 2026-07-14 removal of TROPIC01 and the dual-SE XOR split as the correct response to single-SE compromise. Transferable lessons: (1) a signature verifier whose outcome hinges on one final compare is a single-pulse target even inside an SE with laser sensors — pq1's FSBL c10 verify on an MCU with NO laser/EM sensors must use redundant, Hamming-distant, time-jittered result checking (pq1's EF-swarm F15 'FI-hardened FSBL image verify' gate is exactly this and is still OPEN); (2) SE maintenance/update modes are attack surface — pq1 should document which OPTIGA/SE050 update/maintenance modes are disabled or lifecycle-locked (S-1/S-2/S-3); (3) 'non-persistent' compromise still allows per-boot attacks on a device the attacker holds, so pq1's accepted residual must be stated per power cycle.

claim: Ledger Donjon, 2026-07-09 (disclosed to Tangem 2026-02-10): on the Samsung S3D232A secure element ('certified to EAL6+', ANSSI CC report), a single laser pulse faulted one conditional check in the SetPin handler ('is this card in recovery state?'), letting the attacker set a new password without the old one or a backup card and drain funds; 'EAL6+ certification does not guarantee immunity to fault injection'; bench 'around $250,000'; first success in ~1 h after characterisation, then '100% success rate' ~2 h per card; no firmware update mechanism so it 'cannot be patched'. Recommended: redundant state checks at several points, booleans with large Hamming distance, validation inside the sensitive handler.
relevance: pq1's OPTIGA Trust M V3 and SE050 are EAL6+ parts whose PIN/policy logic (SE050 UserID attempt policy, OPTIGA metadata auth/AutoRef) is applet firmware, not silicon — a single-compare fault in that applet is in scope. pq1's mitigation is structural (XOR split: faulting one SE's PIN check releases only half) and should be stated as such; the wipe-on-10-failures and admin-wipe flows should likewise not hinge on a single SE-side boolean.

claim: Ledger Donjon, 2026-09-18 (disclosed to Raspberry Pi 2026-07-28): on RP2350 A4, photon-emission microscopy located the DEBUGEN register bits, and guided laser pulses set PROC1/PROC1_SECURE to obtain Secure debug despite the 'permanent' CRIT1.DEBUG_DISABLE OTP bit, because DEBUGEN can override it; laser could also set DEBUGEN_LOCK bits, which then prevented software from restoring the disabled state; a rescue reset via the RP-AP cleared the OTP runtime page lock before firmware re-applied it, exposing the OTP secret. OTP flags had 3-of-8 voting, DEBUGEN 'no documented redundancy'; once calibrated the sequence 'enabled Secure debug within seconds'; ~$250k bench; 980 nm 100 ns pulses. Lessons: 'protect every security-relevant control register', 'a software-write lock is not a fault-resistant lock', check reset paths, 'system security depends on that path rather than on individual mechanisms in isolation'.
relevance: Maps onto pq1's STM32U585 trust root: RDP-2 and TZEN live in FLASH_OPTR latches and the debug path goes through DBGMCU/TAMP; pq1's invariant #10 ('RDP-2 freezes option bytes forever') is a latch-integrity assumption without silicon redundancy evidence. Actions: enable ITAMP6 (debug-port access) as a detector; treat 'option byte read-back mismatch' as a wipe trigger not a halt (see Trezor boardloader); document that the FSBL immutability claim depends on WRP/RDP latch integrity under LFI, which no vendor has demonstrated for U5.

claim: Trezor Suite's firmware hash check (since Suite 24.11.2) runs 'every time you connect your Trezor device'; Suite 'presents a mathematical challenge to the device that can be passed only if the official and untampered version of the firmware is present' (device-side GetFirmwareHash = BLAKE2s over the firmware area keyed with the host challenge, modtrezorutils.c); it is skipped when the Suite binary and device firmware versions differ, and on mismatch Suite flags the device 'potentially unsafe' and 'restricts certain functions'. Donjon: the design 'relies on memory that can't be extended and firmware that can't be compressed' and 'we were able to fully bypass this protection' on Safe 3.
relevance: A host-driven firmware hash answered by the firmware itself is a known-bypassable control. pq1's equivalent is the FSBL-measured on-display fingerprint, which is stronger because the measurer is WRP-locked immutable code, but it shares the 'firmware must not be compressible / spare flash must be unusable' assumption for the NS slot — pq1 should either fill/measure the entire slot windows (it measures 'active firmware slots'; confirm unused tail is included) or accept the residual explicitly. Also: do not add a companion-side GetFirmwareHash as a security control.

claim: On STM32U5 fault-injection status: Donjon (2025-03-12) wrote that for Safe 5's STM32U5 'no fault injection attack has been made public at the time of this writing' but that it 'still won't be as secure as a Secure Element' and the improvement may last only 'for a while'; Trezor's spokesperson (June 2026) said no Donjon research identified a vulnerability in the Optiga and the STM32U5 'is a more recent microcontroller with no demonstrated fault-injection attack against it'.
relevance: pq1 shares the U585 with Safe 5/7, so 'no public FI attack on U5' is the same unevidenced assumption both vendors rest on. pq1 should not claim U5 glitch resistance; its differentiator must remain 'no seed bit on the MCU' (invariant #1) plus measurable FI countermeasures. A pq1-run Scaffold/ChipWhisperer campaign on the U585 RDP fetch and the FSBL verify would be a first public data point.

claim: Trezor Host Protocol (THP): Noise_XX_25519_AESGCM_SHA256 handshake with a masked Trezor static key (mask = SHA-256(static_pub || ephemeral_pub)), long-term pairing credentials, and 'Code Entry' pairing = CPace-X25519-SHA512 (draft-irtf-cfrg-cpace-10, Elligator2 generator from the 6-digit code + handshake hash) with a SHA-256 commitment to Trezor's 32-byte secret. Advisory 'Reported on June 22, 2026': 'A host could complete Trezor Safe 7 pairing without using the code shown on the device, by supplying a degenerate value in the pairing key exchange'; fixed in firmware 2.12.2 (2026-07-22) '[T3W1] Discard low-order keys in THP Code Entry pairing'; the spec now asserts cpace_host_public_key != 0^32 and shared_secret != 0^32 'to prevent the host from using low-order points to bypass code entry authentication'. As of 2026-04-07 only CodeEntry is implemented (NFC/QR not).
relevance: pq1 has no host-pairing or encrypted host channel (plain USB HID APDU v2); WYSIWYS on the trusted display is the compensating control, so this is not a gap for signing integrity, but a paired channel would defend seed-wizard/PIN-adjacent flows and BLE if ever added. If pq1 adds one, this is a worked example of the low-order-point class to test (X25519 all-zero shared secret), and of binding the PAKE generator to the handshake transcript.

claim: Trezor's flash PIN-fail counter is explicitly FI-hardened (docs/storage): the old 32-word 0xFFFFFFFF scheme was resettable because 'by manipulating the voltage on the USB input an attacker could convince the device to read the PIN entry counter as 0xFFFFFFFF'; the redesign requires counter values without 'an overly simple binary representation', uses 'two or more different methods of checking the counter value so that an attacker has to mount different fault injection attacks', minimises branches/loops, and stores PIN logs with interleaved 'guard bits' whose positions come from a guard_key constrained to Hamming weight 8-24 (guard_key mod M == C). On blockwise flash (STM32U5) each counter bit is expanded 1->01, 0->10 and the format is checked on read.
relevance: pq1's page-124 attempt counter and page-123 log-structured off-chain counter are flash-held integers read by the boot reconciliation and the sign path. Check that their encodings are not plain erased-state-equals-zero-attempts (an FI read of 0xFF.. must not decode to 'no attempts used') and that the decode uses a redundant check (e.g. 01/10 expansion + format check) — the Kani/Miri work on page-123 covers logic, not fault-model robustness.

claim: CVE-2025-69893 / Trezor advisory 'Reported on September 24, 2025' by Jiwoo Baek & HeeSeok Kim (published 2026-04-14, CVSS 3.1 4.6 AV:P): mnemonic_to_bits(), used to check recovery-seed integrity after unlock, 'was not constant-time and could lead to seed extraction' via a binary wordlist search; the CVE text says 'an attacker with physical access during initial setup can capture one side-channel trace' and apply 'profiling-based deep learning' SCA. Fix (commit 4e6f0dee, firmware 2.10.0, 2026-01-21 'Fixed side-channel vulnerability in BIP-39 mnemonic processing'): Model One removed the check; T/Safe 3/Safe 5 store a binary copy of the seed and switched the wordlist search from binary to linear. Safe 7 and SLIP-39 users unaffected.
relevance: Direct audit item for pq1's BIP-39 crate and seed wizard (word index -> word, word -> index, checksum verification, and the 8-word fingerprint render): any secret-indexed binary search or table lookup over the 2048-word list leaks the index via timing/power; use constant-time (linear scan with CT compare) or avoid word->index conversion on-device after entry. Also reinforces that single-trace profiled DL-SCA on an unlocked device is a vendor-accepted threat model.

claim: Ledger Donjon's 2026 PQC side-channel output: 'The Hidden Risk of Side-Channel Attacks on Post Quantum Cryptography' (2026-04-29) recovers pqm4 ML-KEM key material on an STM32F4 with 'approximately 40 EM traces' collected in 'less than a minute' via chosen-ciphertext CPA on poly_frombytes_mul, recommending masking ('primary defense'), shuffling and desynchronisation; follow-ups 'Non-Profiled Deep Learning Side-Channel Attacks on ML-KEM' (2026-06-11) and 'A Second-Order Side-Channel Attack on Masked Kyber768' (2026-06-26). None of these address SLH-DSA/hash-based signatures.
relevance: pq1's signing primitive is hash-based (C10), so the lattice-specific attacks do not transfer, but the vendor message is that PQ implementations on Cortex-M are SCA-fragile and that masking/shuffling/desync are expected. pq1 already has an F-16 DPA shuffle and 3-source OptRand; a TVLA/CPA leakage assessment of the WOTS+ chain/PRF (secret-seed SHA-256 on the HASH peripheral) with the in-house scared/lascar tooling would answer the obvious reviewer question Ledger is now asking of all PQ wallets.

claim: Trezor supply-chain posture: devices 'ship without firmware' ('If firmware is already installed the device should not be used'); Safe 7 has a 'tamper-evident holographic seal over the USB-C port' plus a screen sticker, Safe 3/5 a seal 'over the connector'; a Safe 3 seal redesign shipped from April 2024 (added UKCA mark, better adhesion); boxes may be wrapped in 'watermarked plastic foil'; guidance is to buy only from official channels because 'you can never tell who may have had access to it before you'. Trezor's own TROPIC01 disclosure states the LFI attack 'cannot be used to create tampered Trezor Safe 7 devices' because it is non-persistent.
relevance: pq1's shipping model is the inverse (factory flashes firmware, ships at RDP-0 so anyone can verify flash+option bytes+OTP over SWD before first power, then first-boot self-locks to RDP-2). That 'verify-before-first-power' step is something neither Trezor nor Ledger offer and is the strongest implant counter in this survey; it should be marketed and tooled (a one-command verifier script + published expected image/option-byte/OTP digests). Trezor's 'ship blank' choice is the alternative that removes trust in the factory image entirely but moves trust to the bootloader keys.

claim: Trezor's bootloader update is executed by the immutable boardloader: a 'UCB' (update control block) points at a new boot header + code; the boardloader checks the header, enforces monotonic_version >= stored minimum ('BOOTLOADER DOWNGRADED'), computes the Merkle root over the new code, verifies the hybrid signature, checks source/destination non-overlap, and only then writes the bootloader area (Model T used an SD-card raw image instead). The bootloader minimum version is written into the secret area, and the secret area is HDP-hidden after boot. Trezor Safe 7 additionally requires that 'Any firmware update must be physically confirmed on the device by the user.'
relevance: pq1's fw_update is a runtime S-world streaming state machine (CMD 20-24) that writes slots while the full secure runtime is live, and its rollback floor (OTP) is 'not implementation-approved'. Trezor's pattern — stage the image, reboot, let the immutable stage verify-then-copy with a monotonic floor held in a hidden region — is an alternative that keeps the writer minimal and PIN-independent; it is relevant to the open Draft 1.1 A/B rollback decision (OTP-first, FSBL is pre-PIN).

claim: Trezor's production TROPIC01 configuration sets every CFG_SENSORS bit to ENTER_ALARM_MODE (PTRNG tests, oscillator monitor, shield, voltage monitor, glitch detector, temperature, laser detector, EM-pulse detector, CPU alert, and bit-flip detectors on PIN verification, SCB, CPB, ECC, R_MEM, EKDB, I_MEM, PLATFORM), and the firmware 'Reset[s] Tropic and retr[ies] command when alarm mode is detected' (#6104); yet Donjon's single-pulse LFI succeeded on positions 'with laser detectors enabled' and 'without ever triggering an alarm'.
relevance: Evidence that SE-side sensors are a bar-raiser, not a guarantee. For pq1 this argues for (a) not relying on OPTIGA/SE050 tamper sensors in the threat model text, and (b) keeping the MCU-side structural defence (no seed bit on either SE alone) as the claimed property. Also: an 'alarm -> reset and retry' policy on the host MCU can mask repeated FI attempts; pq1's SE drivers should count alarms/resets and escalate to lock/wipe rather than silently retry.

claim: Trezor's bootloader keeps 'auto_upgrade' / 'connect_to_host' as volatile secbools and treats fatal workflow errors as evidence of glitching: on WF_ERROR_FATAL it regenerates the BHK (secret_bhk_regenerate) and erases storage ('erase storage if we saw flips randomly flip, most likely due to glitch'), then halts with 'Bootloader fatal error'. The secbool type uses Hamming-distant constants (sectrue/secfalse) and secbool_and() composition is used in fw_check for secmon validation chains.
relevance: pq1 already uses Hamming-distant sentinels and a CfiCounter but its documented response to a detected fault in the sign path is refusal, not escalation. A 'detected fault -> zeroize DHUK-wrapped BHK page / charge an attempt / wipe after N' policy (as Trezor does in the bootloader) raises the cost of repeated glitch characterisation on a stolen device; pq1's three-way PIN consumption is a natural place to charge an attempt on any FI-sentinel trip.

claim: Castelnovi/Martinelli/Prest (PQCrypto 2018, 'Grafting Trees') showed the first fault attack on the SPHINCS framework (SPHINCS, Gravity-SPHINCS, SPHINCS+): a fault during the recomputation of a hypertree subtree causes a W-OTS+ key to sign two different values; ONE faulted signature suffices to build a universal forgery, and the faulted signatures still verify, so the attack is not detectable by the verifier. The authors found no scheme-level countermeasure and recommended classical redundancy.
relevance: This is the attack class pq1's `crypto::c10_sign_verified*` double-compute → ct-compare → verify chain is built against. C10 (h=18, d=2) has the same hypertree structure, so every Type-1/Type-2 sign and the slot-registration path is in scope. Any future 'optimisation' that signs once is a regression to a known single-fault universal forgery.

claim: Genêt (TCHES 2023/2, ePrint 2023/042) extended grafting to SPHINCS+ with randomized signing and to any mix of faulty+valid signatures: with high probability a SINGLE random bit flip anywhere in signing yields an exploitable, still-verifiable signature; the number of queries needed stays within NIST's 2^64 budget for every parameter set. W-OTS+ caching countermeasures are shown ineffective: with c=1 cached top layer the probability a random fault is exploitable is still 0.8972 (128s) / 0.9505 (128f), and layer caching costs 1.43e5 B (128s, c=1) growing to 2.6e6 B (128f, c=4); branch caching with 171 cached branches was still broken (W-OTS+ compromised with p=0.5555 per recomputation). ChipWhisperer-Lite clock glitching on the reference implementation: 1024 queries at ~1/3 fault probability compromised at least one W-OTS+ in all 5 trials (p=0.5877 faulty-only, 0.9714 faulty+valid). Conclusion: 'no other current solution apart from redundancy' — deployments must implement redundancy checks.
relevance: Directly validates the pq1 design choice (RFC 9814 §A.2 / Genêt) and rules out replacing the ~2x signing cost (Type-2 ≈ 6.4–7.2 s on pq1 silicon, so ~14 s doubled) with a W-OTS+ cache. With d=2 only one cacheable layer exists and P(Expl.) stays ≈0.9, so caching is never a substitute for double-compute. The Python oracle + ChipWhisperer tooling in the repo is a ready-made bench harness to measure pq1's own fault-exploitability rate (tools/bench Scaffold exists but no grafting campaign has been run).

claim: IETF RFC 9814 (SLH-DSA in CMS, July 2025) §5 states that checking a signature before releasing it 'is not effective for SLH-DSA' as a fault countermeasure, and that replicating the signature-generation process 'MAY be used'; Saarinen's SLotH paper states the mechanism: a fault in almost any FORS/XMSS hash is simply authenticated by the next XMSS layer, so 'a signature verification check does not protect against fault attacks' during SLH-DSA signing.
relevance: Standards-level confirmation that pq1's 'verify-before-release alone is insufficient' note in CLAUDE.md is correct. Any reviewer proposing verify-only can be pointed at RFC 9814 §5. The same logic means the on-chain verifier gives zero fault protection to the device.

claim: Genêt/Kannwischer/Pelletier/McLauchlan (ePrint 2018/674) mounted the grafting attack in practice with a 'simple voltage glitch' on an Arduino Due (Cortex-M3), collecting enough faulty signatures to create a universal forgery 'within seconds'; caching one-time signatures fully prevents it for stateful schemes (XMSS/LMS) but not efficiently for stateless ones.
relevance: Shows the attack needs only cheap voltage-glitch equipment against a Cortex-M class part — the same adversary class as the STM32U585 bench. The 'cache for stateful' escape hatch does not apply to pq1's stateless slot-selection design (invariant #8).

claim: Amiet/Leuenberger/Curiger/Zbinden (DSD 2020, 'FPGA-based SPHINCS+ Implementations: Mind the Glitch') found the same fault weakness in a hardware SPHINCS+ implementation — gathering enough private information to forge takes 'a matter of seconds'; a sign-then-verify approach does not detect the faulty signature, 'but a full replication of the hardware might make a detection possible'.
relevance: Moving C10 signing into a hardware accelerator or secure element does not remove the need for redundancy; it only moves it. Relevant to any future 'offload signing to the SE' proposal.

claim: Wagner/Wesselkamp/Oberhansl/Schink/Strieder (PQCrypto 2023, ePrint 2023/1572) found a second, independent WOTS fault target: faulting the WOTS CHECKSUM computation renders it useless and yields at least an existential forgery, universal forgery in advanced settings; it affects BOTH signing and VERIFICATION of all current stateful and stateless schemes (LMS, XMSS, SPHINCS+), with vulnerable points identified in the reference implementations.
relevance: Two consequences for pq1: (1) the signer's checksum step is inside the double-compute so it is covered, but (2) the FSBL's on-device C10 VERIFIER (measured boot / fw_update verify) is a signing-independent fault target — a faulted checksum during verification can accept a forged firmware signature. The FSBL verifier is a single pass today; the EF-swarm F15 'FI-hardened FSBL image verify' gate should explicitly include checksum/target-sum recomputation and a redundant verify.

claim: Wagner/Schink/Streit (Fraunhofer AISEC) with Klein/Freud (BSI) published a BSI-commissioned study (5 March 2024) and ePrint 2025/2096 'Laser Fault Injection Attack on the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme': the WOTS fault attack was implemented with laser fault injection on a standard microcontroller, can target verification or signing in LMS/XMSS/SPHINCS+, and the paper presents a countermeasure described as 'easy to implement' that 'significantly increases the effort' for an attacker.
relevance: A national-agency-backed practical LFI result on hash-based signatures on an ordinary MCU; the proposed cheap countermeasure should be read and ported into both the C10 signer and the FSBL verifier (cost is not quantified in the abstract — read the PDF before estimating).

claim: SLasH-DSA (arXiv 2509.13048, 2025) is the first software-only universal forgery on SLH-DSA: Rowhammer-induced bit flips in OpenSSL 3.5.1's signing state give universal forgery for SHAKE-128f (≈1 h hammering), SHA2-128s and SHAKE-192f (≈8 h), followed by minutes-to-an-hour of post-processing; authors call for 'additional implementation hardening or hardware defenses'.
relevance: Confirms that a memory-corruption fault (not just an instruction skip) during signing is exploitable — the two signing passes in `c10_sign_verified` must not share the mutable intermediate buffers, and the ct-compare must compare full 4008-B outputs, not a hash of them, which is what the current design does; worth pinning with a test that corrupts one pass's SRAM state.

claim: Azouaoui/Schneider/Verbakel (NXP, ePrint 2026/759, Apr 2026) propose 'compressed caching' as a scalable, parameterizable grafting countermeasure that stores WOTS+ signatures/public keys in reduced form; it outperforms standard caching 'when less than approximately 256 kB of caching memory is available' and 'can be configured to achieve high fault detection probability' — but no numeric probability is given in the abstract and no comparison to full recompute-and-compare.
relevance: The only post-Genêt alternative to 2x recomputation from an SE vendor team. It is a probabilistic detector, not the deterministic one pq1 has, so it is not a drop-in replacement; it could be a cheaper SECOND layer if the ~14 s double sign ever becomes a product problem. Novelty is academic — not shipped.

claim: Kannwischer/Genêt/Butin/Krämer/Buchmann (COSADE 2018, ePrint 2018/673): first side-channel analysis of XMSS/XMSS^MT/SPHINCS. Timing and SPA 'unpromising'; XMSS DPA resistance reduces to its PRG; for SPHINCS-256 with a BLAKE-256 PRF in hardware, 'at least a 32-bit chunk of the SPHINCS secret key can be recovered' by DPA because the stateless construction reuses the seed across many PRF calls.
relevance: The attack vector is the PRF that expands the secret seed, not the WOTS chains. In pq1 that is sha256("slot_c10_sk_seed"||…) → `c10::keygen` and the per-leaf secret derivation inside sphincs-c10, run on the unmasked STM32 HASH peripheral.

claim: Saarinen (SLotH, NIST PQC 2024 / ePrint 2024/367): an SLH-DSA implementation with CPU hashing 'will rapidly leak the SK.seed master key' — fixed-vs-random TVLA on the first PRF call reached t=24.5 within 1,000 traces, and the thousands of PRF calls per signature all reuse SK.seed and can be combined horizontally; SHA2 parameter sets place SK.seed in the FINAL SHA-256 block (PRF = Trunc_n(SHA-256(PK.seed‖toByte(0,64−n)‖ADRS_c‖SK.seed))). A masked (threshold-implementation) SHAKE256 unit passed a 100,000-trace TVLA; randomized signing 'must be the default', and the paper recommends instantiating two or more independently randomized hardware copies for fault redundancy.
relevance: pq1 computes every secret-seed PRF with `hw::hash` (STM32 HASH peripheral, unmasked) under `hw-sha256`. The TVLA number (t=24.5 @ 1k traces) is the concrete bar: a 1k-trace fixed-vs-random TVLA on pq1's PRF call is cheap to run with the existing Scaffold/Rigol + lascar/scared tooling and would convert 'DPA shuffle (F-16)' from a claim into a measurement. Physical access + many signatures is the exact PIN-brick / 65,536-cap threat model.

claim: Fluhrer (Cisco, NIST PQC 2024 'Side Channel Resistant Sphincs+'): the DPA-sensitive secrets are exactly the SK.prf input to PRF_msg, the inputs/outputs of PRF, and the inputs (sometimes outputs) of F; everything else can be unprotected. His proposal replaces the flat PRF with a 'PRF tree' so no secret is reused across many hash calls, limits to SHAKE parameter sets (threshold-friendly, 1600-bit state), runs 1.7x slower than unprotected, and stays verifier-compatible (standard signatures/public keys) though the private key format is incompatible with FIPS 205.
relevance: pq1 owns both the signer and the verifier (SPHINCsC10Asm.sol), so it is free to restructure the SECRET side (how slot_sk_seed expands to leaf secrets) without touching the wire format or the on-chain verifier — exactly Fluhrer's trick. A PRF-tree derivation would reduce the reuse count of any single secret from thousands to a handful, shrinking the horizontal-DPA surface at ~1.7x cost. Note: changing masterSkSeed expansion would change pubkeys and hence addresses, so it is a pre-launch-only decision (invariant #6). SHAKE-vs-SHA2 is a settled owner decision; the PRF-tree idea is independent of that.

claim: The 2025 SoK on PQC side-channel vulnerabilities (Dobias/Rezaeezade/Chmielewski/Malina/Batina, ePrint 2025/1222) reports that only ONE published side-channel attack targets hash-based schemes relevant to SLH-DSA and that most SPHINCS+ attacks in the literature are fault-injection attacks (excluded from the SoK's scope).
relevance: The SCA literature on hash-based signatures is thin, which cuts both ways: no public break of an SHA-256 SPHINCS+ signer on an MCU exists, but also no public evidence that one resists. pq1 cannot cite prior art as assurance and must produce its own TVLA receipts.

claim: Belenky et al. (FortifyIQ, TCHES 2023/3, 'Carry-based Differential Power Analysis') recover the secrets needed to forge HMAC-SHA-2 for any message from a PURE HARDWARE HMAC-SHA-2 implementation on an FPGA with as few as 30K traces (3% success) and 100% success at 275K traces, without a profiling stage; the method exploits carries of modular additions.
relevance: Directly undercuts any assumption that routing secret-keyed SHA-256 through the STM32U5 HASH peripheral is 'hardware, therefore side-channel safe'. The SPHINCS PRF (secret seed in the last block) is structurally HMAC-like. Order-of-magnitude trace budget (10^5) fits inside pq1's 65,536-per-chain cap only marginally, but the bootstrap key is chain-independent (C×65,536) and horizontal attacks multiply traces per signature.

claim: Lecomte/Maillard/Moran/Renault/Smith (ePrint 2026/2071, 'Soft Analytical Side-Channel Attacks on SHA-2 and HMAC') recover secret SHA-256 inputs and HMAC-SHA-256 keys with bit-level SASCA using Sentential Decision Diagrams for the multi-word modular additions; the HMAC attack needs no control or knowledge of the input; profiling of load instructions used a multi-position EM probe on an STM32F303RET6 running software HMAC-SHA-256.
relevance: Single-trace-class (profiled) SHA-256 attacks on an STM32 are now public; this matters for the SOFTWARE SHA-256 paths in pq1 (sha2 crate at opt-level 3 in QEMU/host-fallback builds and anywhere `hw-sha256` is not in effect) and for the FSBL (which hashes with a known-input image, so less exposed). Reinforces that the HASH peripheral path must be the only one that touches seeds in production.

claim: First-order masked SHA-2 is established but ARX-cost dominated: McEvoy/Tunstall/Murphy/Marnane (WISA 2007) gave the first DPA on HMAC-SHA-2 and a first-order masked implementation; Biryukov/Dinu/Le Corre/Udovenko (CARDIS 2017) improved masked Boolean-share addition (Kogge-Stone) by 14–19% on Cortex-M3 with t-test validated first-order security; Komano et al. (ePrint 2018/934) optimise Coron-style arithmetic↔Boolean conversion for exactly this use (hash functions with modular addition). Picnic's masked hashing (TCHES 2021) reports 1.8x–5.5x masking penalties for hash invocations on Cortex-M4.
relevance: Gives the cost envelope if pq1 ever masks the seed-expansion PRF in software (only the PRF/F calls need masking per Fluhrer, not the whole hypertree): expect 2–5x on those calls, with A2B/B2A conversions the dominant term. This does not reopen the SHAKE-vs-SHA2 decision; it bounds the cost of staying on SHA-2 if masking is required.

claim: μ-Glitch (Saß/Mitev/Sadeghi, USENIX Security 2023 / Black Hat USA 2022): multiple coordinated voltage glitches from a single trigger defeated TrustZone-M on NXP LPC55S69 and RT6xx (four fault targets: SAU, Secure AHB controller, debug register, BXNS), Microchip SAML11, and ST STM32L5 (fault targets: SAU + global TZ configuration; 47 h sweeping search vs >48 h exhaustive; combined success rate 0.0034). On the STM32L5 they had to glitch the PLL configuration to run ≤32 MHz to get past the brown-out detector that otherwise interferes with VFI. Proposed countermeasure: a random preceding delay of 0–9 cycles before each fault target made two successful glitches ~100x less likely.
relevance: STM32U5 is the same Cortex-M33 TZ-M family as L5 (ST AN5347 covers both) and pq1's `sau.rs` SAU/GTZC programming is the exact fault target. Actionable: (1) keep BOR at the highest level and verify it in the option-byte profile — the L5 attack needed to defeat BoD; (2) insert `wait_random()` before each SAU/GTZC/TZSC write AND read back + compare (the `const assert!` arms check the constant, not the live register); (3) the PLL-config-glitch step means the clock-tree setup in `hw::rcc` is itself a fault target that should be read-back-verified.

claim: Bozzato/Focardi/Palmarini (TCHES 2019, 'Shaping the Glitch'): on STM32F373 a single voltage glitch 11 µs after boot start (during RDP option-byte load) downgrades RDP Level-2 to Level-1 (~4% success, ~25 glitches, 2 h parameter search), re-enabling the bootloader and JTAG/SWD — because Level-1 is 'any value other than 0xCC33/0xAA55', so corrupting one bit of the loaded RDP word suffices; downgrade to Level-0 was not achievable and a full dump needed more than FI. On STM32F103 (RDP1) a bootloader-command glitch dumped 128 kB in 1 min at 5% success.
relevance: Invariant #10 rests on RDP-2 being physically permanent; this paper shows an older ST family where the RDP LEVEL is re-derived from flash at every boot and a boot-time glitch can degrade it for that session. No public equivalent on U5 was found (see other findings), but the design response is the same: the FSBL should read back FLASH_OPTR (RDP, TZEN, BOR_LEV, WRP) with the tz-1 tripwire AND re-check later in the secure world, and the first-boot self-lock must assume RDP-2 was reached only after an independent readback.

claim: Ravi et al., 'Firmware Pitfalls: On Compromising Flash Readout Protection in STM32 Devices' (IEEE NEWCAS 2025) report a flaw in RDP Level 1 dubbed 'RDP Freeze' that lets an attacker capture the MCU's internal state (registers and RAM) with cycle-level accuracy, plus firmware recovery via manipulation of the hardware CRC accelerator and cryptographic key extraction, validated on multiple STM32 series.
relevance: Never let a shipped unit sit at RDP-1 (or 0.5): the pq1 first-boot flow goes RDP-0 → RDP-2 (0xCC) directly, which is right. But any bench/EVT unit at RDP-1, and any firmware path that could leave the device at RDP-1 after a failed self-lock, is exposed to full RAM capture — i.e. seed material in S-SRAM. Add 'RDP-1 is a fatal state, wipe' to the first-boot journal recovery contract.

claim: Ledger Donjon reported to Trezor (12 Nov 2024; disclosed March 2025) that on Trezor Safe 3 a voltage-glitching attack on the general-purpose MCU bypasses the device authenticity check and specifically the firmware hash check, enabling a supply-chain implant, while the OPTIGA Trust M secure element 'effectively thwarts any inexpensive hardware attack'; Trezor Suite authenticates only the SE, not the MCU; no seed/PIN was extracted; Trezor Safe 5 is 'not affected because it uses a more recent microcontroller designed to be more resilient'. Trezor says the issue is resolved but neither party published how.
relevance: This is the concrete 'malicious hardware in the FSBL/MCU' scenario the user asked about: SE attestation proves the SE is genuine, not that the MCU firmware is. pq1's answer (verify-once-physically over SWD at RDP-0, then FSBL fingerprint) is stronger than Safe 3's model, but has the same residual Donjon exploited — a glitch during the MCU's own integrity check. Mitigations to pursue: make the MCU-side measurement cross-attested by the SEs (e.g. the SE releases the entropy half only after receiving an FSBL-computed firmware hash that matches a value sealed at first boot), so a glitched FSBL check cannot unlock funds; and FI-harden the FSBL verify (F15).

claim: STM32U5's vendor-documented fault-injection-relevant sensors are the TAMP internal tampers: ITAMP1 backup-domain voltage monitoring, ITAMP2 temperature, ITAMP3 LSE clock-security, ITAMP5 RTC overflow, ITAMP6 JTAG/SWD access when RDP>0, ITAMP7/12/13 ADC4 analog watchdogs 1–3, ITAMP8 monotonic-counter overflow, ITAMP9 crypto-peripheral fault (SAES/AES/PKA/TRNG), ITAMP11 IWDG reset (enumerated in ST's HAL `RTC_INT_TAMPER_1..13` and in Trezor's stm32u5 tamper driver). ST's AN5156 treats power/clock glitching as a typical threat and notes that below a certain voltage normal behaviour cannot be ensured, which 'may signal a fault injection attack'. I found no ST document describing an RP2350-style setup/hold-margin glitch detector on U5.
relevance: pq1's `hw/tamp.rs` already enables the same ITAMP set as Trezor. The unused lever is ADC4 analog watchdogs (ITAMP7/12/13): Trezor enables them but comments that some 'are never triggered' (no ADC configured). Configuring ADC4 in continuous mode on VREFINT/VDD with tight AWD thresholds turns an existing tamper source into a firmware-emulated voltage-glitch detector that wipes via the TAMP path — a cheap, novel-for-wallets improvement on this silicon. It is slow (ADC bandwidth), so it complements rather than replaces code redundancy.

claim: RP2350 (Raspberry Pi) ships four on-die digital glitch detectors (datasheet §10.9): pairs of D flip-flops at physically distant locations, one with a programmable delay line (75%–120% of minimum clock period in 15% steps); any disagreement (loss of setup/hold margin from clock or core-voltage manipulation) resets the switched core domain within one system clock cycle, unlike the brownout detector's limited analog bandwidth; disabled by default and armed via the GLITCH_DETECTOR_ENABLE OTP flag. In the 2025 hacking challenge: Hextree's EMFI found that at the highest sensitivity 'the rate of undetected glitches is still high enough to make attacks feasible with some effort' (double-fault OTP bypass, erratum E21); Courdesses built a custom laser FI rig specifically 'to permit the injection of faults without triggering the glitch detectors' (E24, no mitigation); Cullen glitched the USB_OTP_VDD pin so the OTP guard word 0x333333 was latched, re-enabling debug (E16, no mitigation); Muench skipped one instruction in the USB bootloader to run unsigned RAM code (E20); IOActive read antifuse OTP with FIB passive voltage contrast.
relevance: The best public data point on what a built-in glitch detector buys: it raises cost but EMFI and laser both got through, and a supply-rail glitch on a sub-block outside the detector's domain (OTP) bypassed it entirely. Lesson for pq1: (a) hardware detectors do not retire software redundancy; (b) the OPTIGA/SE050 rails (LDO2_EN/SE1_EN on pq1) and the MCU's VDD/VBAT domains are separate glitch targets — rail-level glitching of the SE bus or of the backup domain holding TAMP/BKP state deserves its own threat entry; (c) datasheet-level design can be emulated: a secure TIM-driven delay-line-like timing canary is the software analogue.

claim: Other vendors now ship on-die glitch detection as a documented security feature: Nordic nRF54L15/LM20 have a GLITCHDET block ('Voltage glitch detectors', a reset source listed alongside brownout) and a TAMPC tamper controller with active shield, CRACEN tamper detector, fast/slow-domain glitch detectors and signal protector that can trigger a system reset (SECTAMPER reset reason); TI CC27xx includes a Voltage Glitch Monitor 'enabled by default during device boot time operations' that can be kept enabled or disabled at runtime 'to mitigate security risks from low-cost and low-effort physical non-invasive fault attacks'.
relevance: Sets the 2025–26 bar for 'general-purpose secure MCU': STM32U585 does not document an equivalent. pq1 cannot change silicon pre-launch, so the gap must be closed in firmware (redundancy, timing canaries, ADC4 AWD) and documented honestly in HARDENING.md as a residual vs. Nordic/TI-class parts; it is also the strongest argument for a future board revision.

claim: NXP LPC55S1x/LPC551x and LPC55S0x/LPC550x ship a Code Watchdog Timer (AN12912): a 32-bit Secure Counter that software adds to at checkpoints (at most one update per basic block) and that is compared at CWT_Start/Stop — 'If a mismatch is detected between the Secure Counter and the value passed to it, it indicates that the execution flow has been altered' and 'a FAULT is generated'; plus an Instruction Timer pre-loaded with slightly more than the expected instruction count that faults if exhausted before service, detecting unauthorised instructions and bounding execution time.
relevance: This is the hardware twin of pq1's `fi::CfiCounter` (7-step gate with Hamming-distant sentinels). The missing half is the Instruction Timer: pq1 can emulate it with a secure-only TIM/DWT CYCCNT window around each FI-critical block (the double-compute compare, gated_unlock pre-commit, SAU setup) and treat over/under-run as a fault — a timing canary that catches clock-glitch and instruction-skip faults that leave the counter intact.

claim: Arm Trusted Firmware-M's Fault Injection Hardening (FIH) library (adapted from MCUboot) implements control-flow monitoring, default-failure values, complex constants, redundant variables (x, x^mask), global failure-loop hardening, random delay (HIGH profile only, needs an entropy source) and duplicated execution, selected by TFM_FIH_PROFILE OFF/LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH (default OFF); its design doc shows simulated instruction skips on the AN521 FVP bypassing SAU/MPC configuration, PSP-limit setting and the NS-entry LSB clear; it warns that compilers 'can eliminate the protection code during optimization' so compiled assembly must be inspected, and gives no measured overhead.
relevance: Two checks for pq1: (1) `fih.rs`/`fi.rs` already mirror these patterns, but there is no CI gate that disassembles the release secure image and asserts the double-read/compare sequences survived LTO + opt-level s (TF-M's explicit warning) — the `rainbow` fault-sweep skill can automate this against the ELF; (2) TF-M's own simulated skip list (SAU, MPC, PSP-limit, NS entry LSB) is a ready checklist for `sau.rs`/`main.rs` NS hand-off hardening.

claim: Trezor firmware (main @ 6ab39e95, 2026-10-07) ships these software FI countermeasures on STM32U5: `wait_random()` — a random-length (`drbg_random8`) delay loop with two volatile counters cross-checked every iteration and after the loop (`error_shutdown("(glitch)")`); a periodic 'RDI' handler that inserts `drbg_random8() + session_delay` waits; `fih_delay()` (0–127 µs random, `no_stack_protector`) wrapped into `fih_ensure()` before every security `ensure()` in the boardloader; a `volatile next_stage_addr` that is 0 by default and only set at the END of `ensure_signed_bootloader()` so a skipped check branches to 0; duplicated `firmware_present`/`firmware_present_backup` secbools and `sigmask`/`sigmask_inv` complements; and TAMP with all internal tampers in 'confirmed' mode (CR3=0 → secrets erased on any tamper) with the ADC4 analog-watchdog tampers enabled but noted as 'never triggered'.
relevance: Benchmark for parity: pq1 has `wait_random`, `FihBool` (val/complement, Hamming-distant constants), `CfiCounter` and `check_true_into_sentinel`, so it matches or exceeds Trezor on the signer. Gaps to verify in pq1's FSBL specifically: default-zero/poisoned jump target set only after the full verify (Trezor's `next_stage_addr` pattern), a random pre-delay before every option-byte/WRP/RDP readback, and a periodic RDI-style jitter during the 4 s fingerprint window and PIN entry so a glitch cannot be timed from the display/USB.

claim: The widely-indexed blog 'CVE-2026-7731: SPHINCS+ Timing Attack [Deep Dive]' is spurious: the CVE record (CVE.org and NVD, published 2026-05-04 by VulDB) is a SQL injection in 'code-projects BloodBank Managing System 1.0' (get_state.php, CWE-89), unrelated to SPHINCS+/SLH-DSA.
relevance: Do not cite it in any pq1 doc or issue; it surfaces in searches for SLH-DSA side channels and would be a claim-vs-source drift of exactly the kind the FV docs guard against.

claim: PDNPulse (IEEE TIFS 2023) detects board-level implants by measuring the unpowered PCB's power-delivery-network impedance profile with a bench VNA (Keysight E5063A, 300 kHz–3 GHz, 1024 points, ~$20 custom probe, 2-port shunt-through) and comparing to a golden profile with a Fréchet-distance threshold set at intra-class mu+3sigma. Reported 100% TPR / 0% FPR on a PoC board (ATtiny85 trigger Trojan, 1 ohm sampling resistor), Arduino Due (3 Trojans, 5 genuine vs 5 malicious boards, multi-port), MSI H310M (4 vs 3) and Intel I350-T4 (3 vs 3); single-port accuracy only 62.2–91.1%; simulated sensitivity down to a 1.8 fF added capacitor and a 0.02 ohm resistor on a 0.2 ohm baseline. Stated limits: batch process variation yields false positives unless multi-batch FD-KNN is used, more decoupling caps hide anomalies, manufacturing flaws are indistinguishable from malice, and it is explicitly 'not designed as a tamper-evident technology' (transient mods escape).
relevance: The strongest published per-unit 'golden electrical baseline' method and it needs zero firmware or board change. For pq1 it maps onto the RDP-0 verify-before-first-power ceremony: the factory (or an independent verifier) records a PDN Z-profile per unit alongside the SWD flash/OTP readout; the FPR caveat means the baseline must be per-batch, not per-design. It is a bench/VNA method, not something the end user can run at home, and it detects implants on the PDN only (a passive SPI logger with its own battery is out of model).

claim: ImpedanceVerif (TCHES 2023/1, Mosavirik, Schaumont, Tajik, WPI) shows that an on-chip circuit-based network analyzer (deployed on commercial FPGA kits without board changes) extracting the PDN frequency response can detect board-level and chip-level tamper events, including 'the proximity of contactless EM probes to the IC package' and 'a slightly polished IC package', using Wasserstein distance as the decision metric; no numeric accuracy or FPR is given in the published abstract.
relevance: This is the self-sensing analogue of PDNPulse: the chip itself measures its PDN and notices an EM probe or a decapped/polished package, i.e. a runtime SCA/FI pre-attack detector. The STM32U585 has no such analyzer, so the pq1 equivalent would be an ADC/TIM-based ring-oscillator or RC-decay measurement of a dedicated net, which is a research spike, not a port. It informs the SE surface too: OPTIGA/SE050 packages being polished for EM/laser FI is the exact event this detects.

claim: PACTOR (Columbia Mingoo Seok lab with Intel, ISSCC 2024) attaches a sensing circuit to the processor–memory PCB traces and periodically scans for 'a change in capacitance that can be as small as 0.5 picofarads' caused by a probe touching the interconnect, then triggers a protection engine (e.g. switch bus traffic to encrypted mode). The first version produced false alarms at high temperature and missed attacks below room temperature; the fix was a temperature sensor that selects the probe-sensing threshold.
relevance: Quantifies what a bus-probe detector must resolve (sub-pF) and documents the main false-positive driver (temperature). pq1's probe-worthy nets are I2C1/I2C4 to the two SEs and SPI1 to the NV3007; the SE buses are already SCP03/Shielded so a probe only yields ciphertext, but a probe/implant on the LCD SPI sees plaintext frames. A detection-then-react design (refuse to render/sign while the line reads anomalous) is the pattern to copy if any capacitance self-sensing is pursued.

claim: Co-planar capacitive asymmetry sensing (Seo, Nath, Das, Ghosh, Sen; DATE 2021) uses four on-chip metal plates whose pairwise capacitances diverge when an EM probe approaches: >17% capacitance change at 1 mm and >45% at 0.1 mm, detecting both E-field and H-field probes (inductive LC-oscillator sensors such as Homma/Miura CHES 2014 cannot see E-field probes); results are Ansys Maxwell FEM simulations, not silicon.
relevance: Defines the state of the art for pre-attack EM-probe detection. It is an IC-design-time countermeasure, so for pq1 it only informs what to ask of a future SE or MCU vendor, and it calibrates expectations: board-level copies using PCB copper plates and the STM32 TSC would be far less sensitive than the simulated on-die numbers.

claim: Golden-chip-free backscattering side-channel clustering (Nguyen, Yilmaz, Prvulovic, Zajic; HOST 2020, DOI 10.1109/HOST45689.2020.9300127) classified 100 FPGA boards carrying 9 dormant Trust-Hub Trojans across 3 benchmarks with '100% accuracy', including dormant Trojans whose trigger is 'as small as 0.19% of the original circuit', using an RF carrier backscattered off the switching circuit; no false-positive rate or manufacturing-variation bound is reported, and a 2025 follow-up (patent US12189760B2) covers clock-related backscatter detection.
relevance: RF-emission implant detection is real but is a lab clustering method over many boards, not a per-unit self-test; its value for PQ1 is as a batch-level receipt (a verifier with an SDR and a carrier can cluster a shipment of pq1 boards) and as a reminder that dormant implants with no power draw still modulate backscatter. The missing FPR means it cannot be sold as a user-facing guarantee.

claim: Near-field microwave CSRR sensing (Sensors 2025, DOI 10.3390/s25134188) places a 4.37 GHz complementary split-ring resonator 3 mm above a 28 nm Spartan-7 package and reads S11 phase with a Mini-Circuits eVNA-63+ (3.5–5 GHz, 1000 points, 500 repeats); it separates powered/unpowered, configured/unconfigured, 100 vs 10,000 vs 20,000-gate chains, a dormant AES-T100 Trojan vs Trojan-free, and placement-only changes 'with high confidence', but reports no detection/FPR counts, needs a repeatable fixture, and assumes a golden sample plus the ability to halt the clock.
relevance: Shows contactless, non-destructive chip-level tamper/Trojan sensing is reachable with a ~$1k eVNA, which is in range for an independent PQ1 verification lab (not the user). It also shows the method's weakness: it is a golden-sample comparison with unquantified FPR, so it belongs in a sampling/receipt program, not in the per-device trust story.

claim: Piliposyan & Khursheed (IEEE Trans. Computers, DOI 10.1109/TC.2022.3230877) detect PCB Trojans powered from legitimate ICs' I/O pins at run time using INA219 high-side current sensors with 12-bit ADC and ~1 mW resolution feeding a One-Class SVM / Local Outlier Factor model on the board MCU (~27 KB for 1258 support vectors): F1 > 99.7% for a 50 mW Trojan, ~0.88 at 5 mW (LOF beats OC-SVM by 8.5% there), with a performance dip around 20–40 mW; the authors state 'ultra-low power passive Trojans, e.g. resistors and capacitors, should be addressed by other techniques such as visual inspection'. Their earlier TETC 2022 paper (sub power monitors per IC + main monitor) claims to be the first PCB power-analysis Trojan detector.
relevance: Gives the honest floor for on-board current fingerprinting: single-mW resolution, so a parasitic SPI/I2C logger drawing hundreds of µW is invisible. pq1 already has rail switches (LDO2_EN/SE1_EN) that isolate the SE rail; adding a shunt + ADC read of the SE rail and LCD rail at boot gives a cheap run-time budget check that only catches active, mW-class implants.

claim: IRIS (Andrew 'bunnie' Huang, arXiv 2303.07406, 2023; automated system 2024) images a chip's lowest metal layers through the silicon backside with ~1050 nm light and a lightly modified CMOS camera, 'even after the chip has been assembled into a finished product', at micron-scale resolution in 'a matter of minutes' per chip on a Jubilee open-source stage; it bounds gate counts ('to within a couple dozen extra flip flops' at 22 nm when paired with scan chains), cannot resolve transistors (IR diffraction limit), needs an exposed mirror-finish backside (WLCSP-style), and is defeated by backside power delivery. Target equipment cost is 'hundreds to perhaps thousands of dollars'.
relevance: The only end-user-affordable non-destructive silicon-level inspection; it only works if the die backside is optically reachable. pq1's STM32U585CIU6 (UFQFPN48) and the OPTIGA/SE050 packages are not WLCSP, so IRIS does not apply to the current board; it is a package-selection input for a future revision and a reason to prefer vendors that publish die images. Pairs with PQ1's verify-once-physically model (invariant #10) as the die-level sibling of the SWD flash readout.

claim: X-ray CT golden-copy comparison exists but not at per-unit scale: Sandia's CALCE/SMTA 2022 work does 'layer-to-layer evaluations of a PCB using differential imagery analysis' against a Golden Copy, motivated by 'high throughput comparisons', but reports that 'varying density of materials and components ... introduce image artifacts' and image-processing errors raise human drive time; the UF implant survey (Harrison, Asadizanjani, Tehranipoor) states x-ray CT 'require[s] hours of image collection and processing time per board' and notes neutron imaging as an alternative with its own limits.
relevance: Rules out CT as the universal per-unit gate for a consumer signer and positions it as a sampled batch receipt (e.g. N boards per lot imaged and published).
