For PQ1 the useful artefact is a published CT of a reference pq1 unit plus Gerbers so third parties can compare, consistent with the open-source-everything policy.

claim: The UF taxonomy paper 'On Malicious Implants in PCBs throughout the Supply Chain' (Harrison, Asadizanjani, Tehranipoor) states that bare-board characterization is 'usually taken once per fabrication run from test coupons' so it gives 'no information about malicious modifications to individual PCBs', that implants adding out-of-band channels 'evade functional or JTAG tests', and surveys two runtime schemes: periodic resistance measurement of critical traces against 'factory-calibrated values' and an on-board TDR between DRAM and CPU that halts memory operations on reflection mismatch, both valid only if 'calibrated by a trusted entity and ... boards are known to be free of Trojans at the time of calibration'. It cites BoardPUF (Wei et al., ICCAD 2015) for PCB-intrinsic authentication.
relevance: Frames the pq1 decision: any per-unit electrical baseline (resistance/TDR/capacitance) is only as good as the trust in whoever calibrates it, which in PQ1's model is the RDP-0 verifier at first power. It also kills the idea that JTAG/boundary-scan or functional self-test can detect a passive listener on the LCD SPI.

claim: Parasitic Circus (Safa, Schaumont, Tajik; arXiv 2403.12252, 2024) tests golden-free PCB verification by simulating the PDN impedance signature from the PCB design files and comparing to measurements on an in-house board; it finds 'the parasitic impedance of the PCB components plays a major role' and that statistical metrics 'mitigate' (not eliminate) the simulation-vs-measurement discrepancy; no accuracy figures in the abstract.
relevance: For an open-hardware signer whose Gerbers and BOM are published, this is the route by which an independent party could verify a pq1 board without trusting a factory-recorded golden sample; the component-parasitic sensitivity means the BOM must pin exact part numbers (which PQ1's reproducible-build ethos already requires for firmware but not yet for passives).

claim: Kuhn (PET 2004, 'Electromagnetic Eavesdropping Risks of Flat-Panel Displays') recovered readable text from a laptop's FPD-Link/LVDS panel link at 3 m (350 MHz centre, 50 MHz IF bandwidth, 57 dBµV/m, 16 frames averaged) and at ~10 m through three plaster walls (39 dBµV/m, 12 frames), because the periodic frame refresh lets the receiver average; the only effective software countermeasure found was adding random bits to glyph colour combinations 'randomly selected each time a new character is placed on the screen', and he warns that a glyph cache that reuses an already-rendered bitmap 'merely assists the eavesdropper'.
relevance: Directly implicates the pq1 NV3007 SPI panel: the MOSI line carries plaintext pixel data on a periodic TE-synced refresh, and the ui-px pixel pilot renders from a fixed, SHA-256-pinned glyph atlas, which is exactly the cached-glyph anti-pattern. Any per-render randomisation must not change the atlas hash the firmware verifies, so the mitigation must sit in the compositor (e.g. randomised low-order pixel values or framebuffer jitter after atlas verification), and the FSBL fingerprint window is likewise a periodic, averageable frame.

claim: Screen Gleaning (Liu et al., NDSS 2021, arXiv 2011.09877) read six-digit 2FA codes from an iPhone 6s display ribbon via a Langer RF-R 400 probe at <1 cm, Minicircuits ZKL-2 amplifier and Ettus X310 SDR (12.5 MHz bandwidth around 295 MHz; other phones at 105/465 MHz): 89.8% per-digit accuracy over 1,200 digits, 50.5% full-code and 99.0% at least-4-digit accuracy; countermeasures listed are shielding the display cable, encrypting the GPU-to-panel link, and a Kuhn-style filtered font, with visual obfuscation noted as 'often ineffective against machine learning'.
relevance: Modern ML-assisted TEMPEST on a small panel link needs only a near-field probe, i.e. an implant-sized antenna inside the pq1 enclosure or a probe pressed on the case would do. It argues for treating the LCD flex/SPI as a protected net (ground-plane shielding, short routing already partly true on pq1's PA4/PA5/PA7) and for randomised PIN keypad layouts, which Ledger already ships (see wallet.fail finding).

claim: Ledger's Donjon threat model: device genuineness is a per-SE keypair signed by Ledger's HSM at manufacturing and challenged on first connect, every Ledger Wallet access, app install and firmware update; it explicitly states 'a Genuine check cannot detect unauthorized physical modifications to the hardware, such as spying implants' if the original SE remains intact, cannot verify 'the device's physical supply chain history', and that holographic/anti-tamper seals 'give a false sense of security' because they are clonable and packages can be reopened without damage; Ledger's stated answer is that signers 'are designed so users can check the integrity of their devices by themselves'.
relevance: The market leader concedes the exact gap PQ1 is asking about and offers only openability as the mitigation. PQ1's SE attestation (OPTIGA/SE050 at boot) has the same blind spot; surpassing Ledger here means pairing attestation with a per-unit electrical baseline (PDNPulse-class) and/or active tamper mesh, and publishing a user-performable open-and-compare procedure with reference photos.

claim: Ledger Stax/Flex are marketed as having the E Ink touchscreen driven directly by the CC EAL6+ ST33K1M5 secure element so that 'a screen driven by an ordinary microcontroller could be vulnerable to spoofing'; however the Donjon threat model lists 'External peripherals: screen, buttons' and its 'Secure Display and Inputs' page does not say which component drives the display nor consider a display-bus implant, screen replacement, or compromised MCU.
relevance: Ledger's WYSIWYS guarantee stops at the SE's display driver output; a tap or substitution on the panel link is out of their published model too. PQ1's position (S-world MCU drives the panel; atlas hash verified before and after each dialog) is comparable but not stronger on the physical link; the differentiator PQ1 can claim is the FSBL-anchored measured boot of the renderer, which Ledger does not expose for user verification.

claim: Trezor Safe 3/5/7 device authentication: a unique certificate is issued to the SE on the production line, Trezor Suite sends a random challenge, the OPTIGA (Safe 3/5) or both TROPIC01 and OPTIGA (Safe 7) sign it, and since the May 2026 update Suite also checks 'a signature from the MCU using ML-DSA-44', promoting the STM32U5 'from a coordinator to a third, independently auditable signature layer'; the trezor-firmware tree implements this in core/embed/sec/mcu_attestation/mcu_attestation.c (ML-DSA keypair derived from secret_key_mcu_device_auth, challenge signed with empty context, gated on SECURE_MODE and USE_MCU_ATTESTATION). Ledger Donjon's 12 Nov 2024 evaluation 'successfully reused a previously known attack' (MCU voltage glitch) to bypass Safe 3's supply-chain countermeasures; Trezor states Safe 5 is unaffected because of 'a more recent microcontroller'.
relevance: Trezor already ships a PQ MCU attestation on the same STM32U5 family PQ1 uses, so a PQ attestation leg is table stakes, not a differentiator; PQ1's SPHINCS+C10-only rule means a C10 MCU attestation rather than ML-DSA. The Donjon result shows attestation keyed from an MCU-held secret is only as strong as the MCU's glitch resistance, which is the FI surface PQ1 already treats with DHUK/RDP-2 self-lock; and none of these layers see a board implant.

claim: Trezor's STM32U5 TAMP configuration (core/embed/sec/tamper/stm32u5/tamper.c) enables internal tampers ITAMP1/2/3/5/6/7/8/9/11/12/13 (backup-domain voltage, temperature, LSE CSS, RTC overflow, JTAG/SWD at RDP>0, ADC4 analog watchdogs 1-3, monotonic counter overflow, crypto-peripheral fault, IWDG) in 'confirmed' mode (TAMP->CR3 = 0, 'all secrets all deleted when any tamper event is triggered'), samples external pins at RTCCLK/256 (128 Hz) with a 4-sample filter and 8-cycle precharge, and only the T3W1 (Safe 7) boards define a single passive external TAMPER_INPUT_2; no active (PRNG-driven ATAMP) tamper pair is configured anywhere in the tree.
relevance: PQ1's secure/src/hw/tamp.rs is a port of exactly this internal-tamper set, so PQ1 is at parity with Trezor and neither uses the U5's active-tamper mesh driver. The ADC4 analog-watchdog tampers (ITAMP7/12/13) are the one STM32-native hook that can turn an external analog measurement (e.g. a sense net on the LCD/SE bus or a mesh) into a hardware-enforced secret wipe without software in the loop.

claim: STM32U5 active tamper: RM0456 §64.1 states the active-tamper mode checks that tamper pins are not 'externally opened or shorted'; an ST technical moderator (4 May 2026) confirmed 'the STM32U5 supports protection against both external open-circuit and short-circuit conditions on the tamper line', with the TAMP_OUT pin driven by a hardware PRNG (ATOR register: 8-bit value that must be read twice and only trusted when consecutive reads match; 128-bit seed via ATSEEDR; secure-APB-only) and compared against TAMP_IN; capacitive/inductive sensing is possible only via a user-designed external circuit that converts the change into a voltage on the TAMP pin.
relevance: This is the vendor-shipped primitive for a PCB tamper mesh over the U585 + both SEs that docs/hardware/hardware_requirements.md lists as 'board not started; firmware ext-pin cfg open'. On the 48-pin pq1 the TAMP_IN/TAMP_OUT pin availability must be checked against the STM32U585CIU6 datasheet before committing (PA0 is the LEFT key on pq1), and an active mesh detects cut/short/bypass of the mesh, not an implant soldered to an unmeshed net.

claim: The STM32 Touch Sensing Controller measures electrode capacitance by charge transfer: it charges the sensor capacitance Cx and transfers the charge into a sampling capacitor Cs until Cs reaches VIH, the transfer count being the capacitance measure; ST's AN5105 notes the measured parasitic 'includes the GPIO pad capacitance and the coupling between the electrode tracks and the application ground', and touch is detected as a count delta against a baseline. A NAIST study (IEICE HWS2021-50) reports that output differences of on-IC capacitance sensors between same-model devices come from manufacturing variation in the IC's ADC and the board trace, enough to re-identify an individual PCB. No ST document frames TSC as a bus-load self-test.
relevance: The STM32U585 ships a TSC, so a firmware-only capacitance baseline of selected nets (LCD SPI, SE I2C, NC pins) is feasible without new parts: record counts at the RDP-0 ceremony, re-measure at every boot, and route the comparison into an ADC4 analog-watchdog/ITAMP wipe or a refusal. Sensitivity is finger-scale (pF), so it catches a probe clip or an added IC, not a femtofarad implant, and temperature drift (per PACTOR) is the FPR risk; this is 'unknown' as a security self-test and would be a PQ1-novel claim if validated on pq1 silicon.

claim: wallet.fail (35C3, Dec 2018): researchers installed a hardware implant in an opened Ledger Nano S that electronically 'push[es] the confirmation button when triggered by radio frequency from the attacker', and eavesdropped Ledger Blue PIN entry via an antenna at 'very close distance' with a classifier that needed the receiver, device and USB cable in 'exactly the same' position; Ledger's response called the implant scenario 'quite unpractical', said the Nano S is 'easily openable, so you can check the integrity of the device yourself', and shipped a randomized PIN keyboard on the Nano S with the same planned for the Blue.
relevance: Concrete precedent that a sub-$10 implant inside a hardware wallet can forge user consent on the button line, which attestation and measured boot cannot see. PQ1's chord-click gesture (both buttons down, fire on release) raises the bar slightly over a single-button press; a tamper mesh over the button nets, or sampling button analog levels through ADC4 watchdogs, would be the direct countermeasure. Randomised PIN keypad is a cheap, already-shipped SCA mitigation PQ1's S-world PIN entry should match.

claim: Supermicro-style implants: Bloomberg's 4 Oct 2018 'Big Hack' claim was denied by Apple, Amazon, Supermicro, DHS and the UK NCSC; Supermicro's Dec 2018 customer letter reported a third-party review (Nardello & Co., per Reuters/TechCrunch sources) found 'absolutely no evidence of malicious hardware' on sampled current-production boards and boards sold to Apple/Amazon; independently, Trammell Hudson's 35C3 'Modchips of the State' demonstrated 'a proof of concept SPI bus hardware implant' with similar capabilities on a BMC and discussed detection countermeasures, and the UF survey cites a PoC that replaced a resistor on a BMC memory bus with a small FPGA to alter firmware.
relevance: The attack class is proven even though the headline incident is unverified: SPI/memory-bus interposers that alter boot code. PQ1 is structurally resistant because there is no external SPI flash; the FSBL and both slots live in internal flash measured at boot, and the SE links are encrypted. The remaining SPI net is the display, which is a read-only sink for plaintext, so the implant threat on pq1 is exfiltration/consent-forgery, not code injection.

claim: SentryBus (arXiv 2608.17082, 2026) models I2C sensor-interface manipulation by 'an inline interposer, parallel controller, sensor replacement, or compromised host' using host-visible transaction timing, read/write sequences, transfer lengths and address behaviour; on a dual-sided testbed an inline interposer was 'bounded at 0.842 percent of acquisition service time', clean acquisition was stable over 6304 s, data-transition features 'did not transfer across capture sessions', and 'no detection rate is claimed' because controlled attack trials are outstanding.
relevance: The most recent attempt at host-side I2C interposer detection shows the signal is tiny (<1% timing overhead) and session-unstable, so timing fingerprinting of the OPTIGA/SE050 I2C buses would be a weak detector for pq1. The practical defense remains what PQ1 has: SCP03 and Shielded Connection with per-device final keys, which turn an interposer into a DoS/attempt-burning adversary rather than a reader, plus the page-124/E120 attempt reconciliation that already bounds that.

claim: 'Analog Pin Directionality as an Exfiltration Attack Surface in Mixed-Signal ICs' (arXiv 2609.19111, submitted to IEEE TIFS) shows a hardware payload below 0.001% area in a 55 nm PPG analog front-end can turn a nominally input-only analog pin into an outbound channel at up to 10 kbps via data-dependent offset modulation, with only 0.03 dB SNR cost, 5.9% max perturbation versus 34.3% benign PVT variation, raw SINR below -20 dB but above 14 dB after targeted filtering; enabling conditions are a closed-loop amplifier, exposed amplifier input and high pin impedance.
relevance: An in-IC Trojan can exfiltrate through pins that firmware treats as inputs or NC, so a 'no extra parts on the board' audit is insufficient; on pq1 the exposed high-impedance analog-capable pins (PA6 is NC/mask, ADC inputs) are candidates. Mitigations within PQ1's reach are terminating unused pins, keeping secrets off the MCU ADC path, and treating the SE-rail/analog nets as part of any RF-emission sampling receipt.

claim: Purism's Anti-Interdiction Service (2019) ships laptops with customized tamper-evident tape on the sealed bag and inner box, glitter nail polish on the bottom-case screws, photos of the sealed measures and the laptop interior sent 'out-of-band, signed by Purism and encrypted against the customer's GPG key', and optionally ships the Librem Key separately or delays the laptop until the key arrives; Purism states 'we don't claim to prevent interdiction', only to detect it.
relevance: A shipped, low-tech per-unit golden baseline (unclonable glitter pattern + signed interior photo) that addresses the transit implant window attestation cannot. It composes directly with PQ1's RDP-0 verify-before-first-power ceremony: the verifier photographs the opened pq1 and seals it; the user compares before first power. Cost is per-unit labour, not silicon.

claim: Trezor ships tamper-evident packaging: Safe 3 has 'a holographic seal over the USB-C connector' that leaves a 'VOID' residue when removed, Safe 5 guidance is to confirm the package is intact and the connector seal unbroken, and the outer box may carry a Trezor-watermarked foil 'to make it easier for customers to verify that their device is genuine'; this is the opposite stance from Ledger Donjon, which says such seals 'give a false sense of security' and are trivially cloned, and from the wallet.fail researchers who reported removing seals with a hair dryer.
relevance: Seals are cheap and users expect them, but the two incumbents disagree on their value and the attack (re-seal) is documented. PQ1 should not stake a security claim on seals; if used, pair them with a signed photo baseline (Purism model) and the user-side SWD/fingerprint verification so the seal is a convenience, not an assurance.
